pages.text:
STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
4. The harsher lines in Vosper’s editorial
The Coolgardie Miner of 16 June 1894, as quoted by Kabir (2009), also said: “We fear that a low
degenerate mongrel race of human beings will follow where they lead, and for the protection of our
Anglo-Saxon race we say and say emphatically ‘ooshtah’…” That sentence is kept off the Year 5–6
witness card. Teachers may choose to unpack it here. It is racist language, printed as an editorial, and
it is part of the record.
Question. If a source is ugly, what is the difference between quoting it to understand a campaign, and
repeating it as if it were ordinary talk?




STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
5. The Canning Stock Route
Cameleers worked on the Canning Stock Route. The survey and well-sinking also involved Aboriginal
people, including forced guiding and serious harm. This file does not pretend to tell that story on the
student pages. Teach it with AIATSIS guidance.
Question. Why might a case about cameleers still have to leave part of the route story open, and who
should be consulted before it is taught in full?




STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
6. The dictation test and the door that closed
The Immigration Restriction Act 1901 did not always name a race in the test itself. Officials could
choose the language of the test. Cameleers who had lived in Australia for years were still refused
naturalization, as Faiz Mahomet was in 1896, even before the Commonwealth Act. After 1901, leaving
to visit family could mean not getting back in.
Question. Is a law that never uses the word “Afghan” still a way of pushing people out? What
evidence in this file helps you answer?




STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
7. Trucks, and what “the period of usefulness” meant
From the 1920s motor trucks took over much of the inland carting. Some later writers have used
phrases such as “the period of usefulness has passed.” Usefulness to a colony is not the same thing as




                         Reopen the Record: Australian Histories · sample ·   120

belonging in it. Some cameleers left; some stayed; some married European or Aboriginal women, and
their families remain.
Question. If a group is valued while their work is needed, and shunned when the work changes, what
does that tell you about whether they were ever welcomed?




8. Sure, maybe, or a guess?
Sure: Elder imported camels in 1862; Faiz and Tagh were on the Western Australian goldfields from
1892; Vosper’s paper printed the 16 June 1894 editorial; the Immigration Restriction Act was passed
in 1901. Maybe: the exact wording of every line of Musakhan’s 25 April letter, until a teacher checks
the Trove page word for word. A guess: how any one unnamed cameleer felt on a particular night on
the track. The opening scene is not evidence.
Question. Take one sentence from the opener, one from “What is agreed,” and one from a witness
card. Mark each sure, maybe, or a guess — and say why.

pages.text:
Teacher Note
THE ‘AFGHAN’ CAMELEERS · YEAR 5–6 · TEACHER NOTE


This note is for the teacher. It is not a student page.


What’s true about the opener
The typographic page is a constructed scene, written for this file. It is not a quotation, and not a
named person’s diary. The handover line about tracks and whether the country opened to the
cameleers is this file’s framing. What’s true sits in “What is agreed,” the witness cards, and this
note.


Curriculum
The brief asked for an accurate AC9HS5 code. The lead code is AC9HS5K03: the role of a
significant individual or group, including those who migrated to Australia, in the development
of events in an Australian colony. The Immigration Restriction Act and citizenship after
Federation also sit under AC9HS6K02. Both codes are used. There is no Year 5–6 “AC9HS9”
code; that numbering belongs to later History courses, which use AC9HH.


Source conflicts, flagged
Faiz Mahomet’s arrival is given as about 1870 (ADB) and as 31 December 1865 (some later
accounts). Musakhan’s year of death is given as 1939 in some accounts and 1945 in others. The
25 April 1895 West Australian wording is taken from later historical quotation, not from a fresh
Trove transcription by this file; it should be checked if a teacher has the page. The “Sons of God”
sentence sometimes attached to Faiz after the Coolgardie food shortage of 1893 is cited to Brian
Willis (1992) in later retellings. This file has not verified that sentence in a primary source, and
does not use it on student pages.


First Nations, and consultation
Teach it with care, following AIATSIS guidance and local community protocols. The Canning
Stock Route, and marriages with Aboriginal women, are First Nations histories as well as
cameleer histories. Teach with AIATSIS guidance. Do not treat the stock-route survey and well-
sinking as a colourful extra. The student pages name the route and leave the harm in this note,
on purpose.


Religion, names, and care
Most of the cameleers were Muslim. Teach the faith with respect. The word “Afghan” is
explained as a settler label. Vosper’s editorial uses racist language; the harshest sentence is kept
for this note and for Super Sleuths, so Year 5–6 teachers can decide how to handle it.

School of Arts, Tenterfield
                                                                      Thursday, 24 October 1889

The great question which they had to consider was, whether the time had not now
arisen for the creation on this Australian continent of an Australian Government, as
distinct from a local Government and an Australian Parliament.

Surely what the Americans had done by war, the Australians could bring about in
peace.

He believed that the time had come, and if two Governments set an example, the
others must soon of necessity follow.

The thing would have to be done, and to put it off would only tend to make the
difficulties which stood in the way greater.

                                            Queen’s Hall, Parliament House, Melbourne
                                                                                 6 February 1890

            The crimson thread of kinship runs through us all.

Who had a say in making the nation, and who was
left out?
Federation, 1901

 A NOTE BEFORE YOU READ
 Teach it with care, following AIATSIS guidance and local community protocols. This file asks who
 was left out of the new nation, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. Teach it with
 care, and follows AIATSIS guidance. A note for teachers is at the end of the case.




He never saw it happen.
                               Sir Henry Parkes died in Sydney on 27 April 1896.
                               The Commonwealth of Australia came into being on 1 January 1901, at a
                               ceremony in Centennial Park, Sydney. He was not there. The words on the
                               previous page are from 1889 and 1890. They are not a speech from 1901,
                               and this file does not give him a voice he did not live to use.

    Barnett. Public domain.

 April 1896)

pages.text:
WHAT IS AGREED · FROM THE 1889–1902 RECORDS, AND AFTER
  Sir Henry Parkes, five times Premier of New South Wales, spoke at a banquet in the School of Arts at
  Tenterfield on 24 October 1889. He called for an Australian government and an Australian parliament,
  and for a convention to draw up a constitution. The next morning, The Sydney Morning Herald printed a
  long report of the speech, mostly in reported speech — “he said,” “they had to consider” — not as a word-
  for-word script in the first person.

  On 6 February 1890, at a banquet in Melbourne for the Australasian Federation Conference, Parkes
  responded to the toast “A United Australasia.” The line most often remembered from that night is: “The
  crimson thread of kinship runs through us all.” In the same speech he spoke of a shared British origin.
  That “us” did not include everyone who lived on this continent.

  Parkes died in Sydney on 27 April 1896. He did not see 1 January 1901, when the Commonwealth of
  Australia came into being at a ceremony in Centennial Park, Sydney. Edmund Barton became the first
  Prime Minister.

  The Constitution had been agreed to in referendums, colony by colony, in 1898, 1899 and 1900, and then
  passed by the British Parliament. Who could vote in those referendums was not the same in every colony.
  In most colonies the voters were adult men. Women could already vote in South Australia, and, from 1899,
  in Western Australia, and they could take part in the later referendums there. Aboriginal people were not
  treated the same way in every colony. In Western Australia, and in Queensland, most Aboriginal people
  were kept off the roll. The picture is more complicated in some other colonies, and this file does not
  pretend it was simple.

  The Constitution, as it stood in 1901, said two things that matter for this case. Section 127 said that, in
  reckoning the numbers of the people, “aboriginal natives shall not be counted.” Section 51(xxvi), the “race
  power,” gave the Commonwealth Parliament power to make special laws for “the people of any race, other
  than the aboriginal race in any State.” Both provisions were later changed, in 1967. This file does not treat
  1967 as the end of the story.

  On 12 June 1902 the Commonwealth Franchise Act became law. It gave the federal vote to men and
  women who were twenty-one or over, British subjects, resident, and on the roll — and then shut many
  people out. It said: “No aboriginal native of Australia Asia Africa or the Islands of the Pacific except New
  Zealand shall be entitled to have his name placed on an Electoral Roll unless so entitled under section
  forty-one of the Constitution.” Section 41, and how it was later read, is still argued over. In 1901 the new
  Parliament also passed the Immigration Restriction Act, which used a dictation test to keep many people
  out.

  New Zealand did not join the Commonwealth. Parkes had spoken of “Australasia” at the 1890 banquet; the
  nation that began in 1901 was the six Australian colonies.




Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber, used in Super Sleuths, marks what is still disputed or was
added later.

Australia. Public domain.   line is often later attached to 1 January 1901. This file keeps it in 1897, where the record

Mei Quong Tart
                              Chinese-Australian merchant and community figure, Sydney · Died 1903
                              A well-known Sydney merchant, he wrote to the first Prime Minister about how the new
                              Commonwealth’s immigration law was affecting Chinese people.
                              Source. The National Archives of Australia holds a letter from Quong Tart to Edmund Barton, dated 8
                              January 1903, about the Immigration Restriction Act 1901 — including domicile certificates, the education
                              test, and state deposits. This card summarises what that archive record is, and does not invent sentences
                              from a letter this file has not transcribed word for word. The photograph is a real portrait of about 1900,
                              National Library of Australia, public domain (taken before 1 January 1955). No likeness has been invented.
Mei Quong Tart, about 1900.
    National Library of
                              What they said. On 8 January 1903, two years after the Commonwealth began, he wrote
 Australia. Public domain.    to Prime Minister Barton about the way the Immigration Restriction Act was being used
                              against Chinese people. The Archives describe the letter as dealing with domicile
                              certificates, the education test, and state deposits. The education test — the dictation test —
                              was the device the 1901 Act used to keep many people out, without always naming a race in
                              the test itself.
                              Could they really have seen it? He lived in Sydney, and he had standing in both Chinese and
                              European circles. He could describe what the new law was doing to people he knew. He wrote
                              after 1901, not at the Centennial Park ceremony, and not as a voter who had been invited to help
                              write the Constitution. He also cannot be made to stand in for Aboriginal people, whose
                              exclusion was written into other clauses.
                              Why might they say it? To ask the first Prime Minister to look at how the new nation’s law
                              was falling on Chinese residents and travellers. A letter to Barton is evidence of a protest, and of
                              who had to ask. It is not the same thing as having had a say in 1899 or 1900, when the
                              Constitution was put to the referendums.

My finding
FEDERATION · YEAR 6

The three witness cards are Edmund Barton, Rose Scott, and Mei Quong Tart. Further questions — including who
could vote in the referendums, section 127, the 1902 Franchise Act, and what “us all” included — are in Super
Sleuths.

There is no answer at the back. The records show that some people had a vote, and that some
people were written out of the count and out of the roll. They do not capture every voice that
was never asked. Write only what these records can support. Do not invent what they do not
say.

Who had a say in making the nation, and who was left out?
Circle one: Everyone who lived here had a say · Some people voted, and some were written out of
the Constitution and the roll · The speeches tell the whole story · We can’t know, from this file,
whose voices were never written down · Another finding, written below


  MY FINDING
  My finding. ________________________________________________
  ______________________________________________________________
  The one piece of evidence that most changed my mind. ________
  ______________________________________________________________
  What I still can’t know. ___________________________________
  ______________________________________________________________




Why it still matters
The speeches still tell us who was meant by “us all.” The Constitution, and the Franchise Act
that followed, still show who was counted, who could vote, and who was left out. Section 127,
and the wording of the race power, were later changed, in 1967. The franchise later widened.
Those changes matter, and they do not close the file. The question of who gets a say in the
nation is not only a question about 1901.

FEDERATION · YEAR 6 · SUPER SLEUTHS
Super Sleuths
Go further only if you want to. Amber marks what is still disputed, or what later writers added. This
file uses published, cited public records wherever it touches First Nations histories.
Open these investigations in the app: robmac10.github.io/federation-case/#sleuth


  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  1. The Herald’s Parkes, not a rewritten “I”
  The typographic page follows The Sydney Morning Herald of 25 October 1889, p. 8. The speech was
  given on 24 October. The Herald mostly used reported speech: “the great question which they had to
  consider was…” Later retellings, including some museum pages, turn this into first person (“we have
  to consider”). This file does not make that change.
  Question. Why might a later writer change “they” to “we,” and what is lost when that happens?




  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  2. “The crimson thread of kinship”
  This line is from the Melbourne banquet of 6 February 1890, not from Tenterfield. In the same
  speech Parkes spoke of a shared British origin. “Us all” was a claim about kinship. It was not a claim
  that every person on this continent was included. Aboriginal people, and many Chinese-Australians,
  were outside that “thread” as Parkes drew it.
  Question. If a speaker says “us all,” how can you tell who is meant?




  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  3. He never saw it happen
  Tenterfield, 24 October 1889. Melbourne banquet, 6 February 1890. Parkes died on 27 April 1896.
  The Commonwealth began on 1 January 1901. The handover line in this file is not a quotation from
  Parkes. It is this file’s plain statement of those dates.
  Question. Why might it matter that the man later called the “Father of Federation” — a later title, not
  a name he gave himself on the typographic page — never saw the ceremony?




  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  4. Who could vote in the referendums
  The Constitution was put to voters in 1898, 1899 and 1900. The rules were not the same in every
  colony. Women could vote in South Australia, and, from 1899, in Western Australia. In most other




                           Reopen the Record: Australian Histories · sample ·   133

pages.alt: Page 134. Federation. colonies the voters were adult men. Aboriginal people were widely excluded in Queensland and Western Australia. In some other colonies the picture is more complicated, and summaries sometimes flatten
pages.text:
colonies the voters were adult men. Aboriginal people were widely excluded in Queensland and
Western Australia. In some other colonies the picture is more complicated, and summaries
sometimes flatten it. New South Wales’s 1898 result is often told as a majority that still failed a
special threshold; later votes went the other way. Western Australia voted in 1900. New Zealand did
not join.
Question. Why is “the people voted for Federation” too simple a sentence?




STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
5. Section 127, and the race power
Section 127 of the Constitution, as it stood in 1901, said that in reckoning the numbers of the people,
“aboriginal natives shall not be counted.” Section 51(xxvi) gave the Commonwealth power to make
special laws for “the people of any race, other than the aboriginal race in any State.” Both were
changed in 1967. This file does not treat those later changes as if they cancelled the 1901 record, or as
if they ended every question about who counts.
Question. What is the difference between not being counted, and not being allowed to vote?




STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
6. The 1902 Franchise Act, and section 41
The Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902, assented to on 12 June, gave the federal vote to men and
women who met its tests — and then said: “No aboriginal native of Australia Asia Africa or the
Islands of the Pacific except New Zealand shall be entitled to have his name placed on an Electoral
Roll unless so entitled under section forty-one of the Constitution.” Section 41 is a difficult clause.
Later governments and courts often read it narrowly. This file flags that dispute rather than settling
it.
Question. Why might a law that is remembered for giving women the federal vote also be a record of
who was shut out?




STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
7. Quong Tart’s letter, and the dictation test
The Immigration Restriction Act 1901 used a dictation test to keep many people out. On 8 January
1903 Quong Tart wrote to Barton about how that law was affecting Chinese people. The National
Archives of Australia describes the letter; this file has not printed a word-for-word extract, because it
has not checked a full transcription against the original in this build. In 1894, Sir Henry Parkes had
written a letter of introduction for Quong Tart, praising his “energy and integrity.” Parkes’s “crimson
thread” and Parkes’s respect for one Chinese-Australian merchant can both be in the record.




                         Reopen the Record: Australian Histories · sample ·   134

STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
8. Barton’s line, and the day it was not said
“For the first time in history, we have a nation for a continent and a continent for a nation” is
recorded as Barton’s line at Ashfield in 1897. It is often later told as if it were said at Centennial Park
on 1 January 1901. This file keeps the 1897 date. A famous phrase can still be the wrong proof for a
day.
Question. Why might people want a great sentence to have been said on the nation’s first morning?

pages.text:
FEDERATION · YEAR 6 · TEACHER NOTE
Teacher Note
Teach it with care, following AIATSIS guidance and local community protocols. This case asks
who was left out of the new nation, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people.
Teach it with care. Follow AIATSIS guidance, and do not treat this file as a finished account of
First Nations experience.


What is quoted, and what is framing
The typographic page is not a facsimile of a newspaper, and it is not a diary. It is a typographic
setting of verified wording. The Tenterfield lines are taken from The Sydney Morning Herald,
25 October 1889, p. 8, which reported the banquet speech of 24 October. The Herald used
reported speech. This file keeps “they had to consider,” “had done,” “could bring about,” and
“He believed that the time had come.” It does not rewrite those lines as “I” or “we.” Some later
museum and classroom pages do make that change. The Teacher Note flags them, rather than
following them.
The last line on the typographic page, “The crimson thread of kinship runs through us all,” is
from Parkes’s response to the toast “A United Australasia” at the Federation Conference
banquet in Queen’s Hall, Parliament House, Melbourne, on 6 February 1890. It is not from
Tenterfield. It is one of the most widely attested sentences in the Federation story. Teachers
should still check a contemporary report (The Argus or The Age, 7 February 1890, or a careful
later printing) beside this page.
“He never saw it happen” is this file’s handover. It is not a quotation from Parkes. The dates
under it are not in dispute: he died on 27 April 1896; the Commonwealth began on 1 January
1901. The file does not invent a Centennial Park scene in his voice, or a child’s invented diary of
that morning, on the student pages.


Care, and conflicts this file will not settle
Who could vote in each referendum is not a single rule. Women voted in South Australia, and in
Western Australia from 1899. Aboriginal voting was restricted or denied in Queensland and
Western Australia; elsewhere the picture is more complicated, and secondary summaries
sometimes flatten it. Section 41 of the Constitution, and how it was later applied to people
already on a state roll, is still argued over. The 1902 Act’s exclusion is quoted from the Act itself
(assented 12 June 1902). “Father of Federation” is a later title. Barton’s “nation for a continent”
line is kept at Ashfield, 1897, not moved to 1 January 1901. This file summarises Quong Tart’s 8
January 1903 letter from the National Archives’ description; it does not print a word-for-word
extract, because a full checked transcription of that letter was not in hand for this build.
Parkes’s 1 March 1894 letter of introduction for Quong Tart is in the State Library of New South
Wales papers.
Rose Scott’s card does not invent a quotation. A later parliamentary-library account has been
cited elsewhere for words of hers about race, colour, and the 1902 franchise. Those words were

IMAGINED Written for this case, based on real events, not a real document.
                                  A notebook, opened more than a century later
                                                         New Year’s Day, 1915 — and now
They packed for a picnic.
That’s the bit I can’t get past. Ore wagons with benches in them.
Sandwiches. About a thousand people going to Silverton, and a
girl my age on the train, sitting next to someone she liked.
They saw an ice-cream cart by the line, and a flag, and two men.
Some of them thought the shots were for the new year. Then the
shots weren’t.
Four people were killed. Seven were hurt. That night a crowd
burned the German Club, and the police had to stand in front of a
mosque so the same crowd wouldn’t go there next.

 I keep looking for a clean reason. The notes they left
don’t give me one I can live with. Neither does what the
                     town did after.

A NOTE BEFORE YOU READ
  This file includes a shooting in which four people were killed, and a riot that night against German
  and Muslim residents. Teach the violence with care. The opening notebook is written for this file;
  what’s true sits in the teacher notes. A note for teachers is at the end of the case.




THE BATTLE OF BROKEN HILL, 1915 · YEAR 9 · READ
The Battle of Broken Hill, 1 January 1915
Why did they do it, and was the backlash fair?


What is agreed
Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber, used in Super Sleuths, marks what is still disputed or was
added later.


  On the morning of 1 January 1915, a picnic train left Broken Hill for Silverton for the annual
  Manchester Unity Oddfellows picnic. The Barrier Miner, printed the same day, said the train left
  Sulphide-street station at 10 a.m., and that it consisted of two brake vans and 40 ore trucks,
  “with a freight of some 1200 picnickers on board.” Some later accounts say 41 carriages. This file
  records both, and does not choose.




  Beside the line, an ice-cream cart was flying a small red flag with a white crescent and star — the
  Ottoman (Turkish) flag. Two men, later named as Gool Badsha Mahomed (the spelling of his
  name varies) and Mullah Abdullah, fired on the train. Four people were killed: Alma Priscilla
  Cowie, aged 17, a passenger; William John Shaw, aged 46, a passenger; Alfred Millard, who was
  riding a bicycle beside the line (his middle name is given as Elton in the NSW Police Gazette and
  some official reports, and as Elvin in some later accounts); and James Craig, aged 69, who was
  in his yard and was hit during the later gunfight, not on the train. Seven other people were
  wounded, including Constable Robert Mills.




  Police, military men under Lieutenant Resch, and armed civilians pursued the two men to a
  quartz outcrop later known as White Rocks. Both men were shot. Abdullah was found dead.
  Gool was badly wounded and died in hospital. Sources disagree on how long the gunfight lasted:
  about 40 minutes in one later museum account; almost two hours in others.




  Notes were found. Contemporary reports and later summaries do not all give the same wording.
  They agree that the notes linked the attack to the Ottoman Sultan and to the writers’ faith, and

that Abdullah’s note also named a grudge against Chief Sanitary Inspector Cornelius Brosnan,
who had prosecuted him for slaughtering animals away from the licensed abattoir. Gool’s note is
widely reported to have been written for him by Abdullah, because Gool was illiterate. This file
has not inspected the original notes.




That night a crowd in Broken Hill attacked and set fire to the German Club. Police later
described the building as “maliciously set fire to and destroyed.” The club’s trustees offered a
reward of £25; the state government matched it. Police and military were also sent to the North
Camel Camp and the mosque, after a crowd moved in that direction. Officers later returned to
the mosque because they had entered it without removing their boots.




Local Muslim residents were threatened. The two men’s bodies were buried by police at an
undisclosed place. A coronial inquest on the four victims opened, was adjourned, and was held
on 7 January 1915; an inquiry into the deaths of Gool and Abdullah followed the next day. The
coroner found that the four had died from gunshot wounds feloniously inflicted by the two men,
and that the shooting of the two men was justifiable.




Gool and Abdullah were Muslim men who had lived at the cameleers’ camp. Police records and
newspapers did not agree on their nationality, and often called them Turks because of the flag.
Later accounts describe Abdullah as probably from Afghanistan or a neighbouring region,
literate in Dari, and Gool as an Afridi man from the Tirah region who had earlier served in the
Ottoman army and, by 1915, sold ice-cream in Broken Hill. The Ottoman Empire had entered
the war against Britain in late October 1914.

Ask the same three questions of each.

                                   in The Barrier Miner, 1 January 1915

                                   The Barrier Miner reported that the two men “attracted the attention of Mr.

My finding
THE BATTLE OF BROKEN HILL, 1915 · YEAR 9 · DECIDE

The three witness cards are M. Kenny, the notes the two men left, and the police record of that night. Further
people — including Walhanna Asson, Cornelius Brosnan, and the local Muslim community — are in Super Sleuths.

You have a constructed notebook, a short agreed file, and three witnesses. The opening page is
not a 1915 diary. Say what you think the records can prove about why the two men fired, and
whether the town’s answer that night was fair. “We can’t know” is an honest finding when the
notes conflict, or when the record of the riot is thinner than the record of the shooting. Do not
invent what the sources do not say. Treat the dead, and the living families of this story, with
care.

Why did they do it, and was the backlash fair?
Circle one: They did it as an act of war for the Ottoman Sultan · They did it because of a local grudge
and years of being shut out · Both of those things were tangled together, and we can’t separate them
cleanly · The backlash was not fair, even if the shooting was a crime · We can’t know, from this
file, all of why they did it, or how far the town’s anger spread · Another finding, written below


  MY FINDING
  My finding. ________________________________________________
  ______________________________________________________________
  The one piece of evidence that most changed my mind. ________
  ______________________________________________________________
  What I still can’t know. ___________________________________
  ______________________________________________________________




Why it still matters
The “Battle of Broken Hill” is still told as a curiosity of the First World War on Australian soil,
and sometimes as if it were simple. The file is open because the notes do not all say the same
thing, because a picnic train is not a battlefield, and because the night that followed — a burned
club, a guarded mosque, a secret burial — is part of the same case. How a town answers a crime,
and who it answers it upon, still matters.

STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
4. James Craig was not on the train
Three people were killed in the attack on the train and the pipe track: Alma Cowie, William Shaw,
and Alfred Millard. James Craig was in his yard, about a hundred yards from the Cable Hotel, and
was hit during the later gunfight. A stepdaughter urged him to come inside. Treating all four deaths
as if they happened in the ore wagons flattens the day.
Question. Why does it matter, for a finding, where each of the four was when they were hit?




STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
5. Walhanna Asson, and the camel camp
Walhanna Asson, a Punjabi-speaking camel-owner from Peshawar, carried water to a wounded
constable while under fire, and was himself nearly shot by late-comers who took him for “one of the
enemy” until police protected him. That night a crowd moved on the mosque. Officers later went back
because they had entered it in boots. Local Muslims protested when a gravedigger began two graves
in their cemetery for the two attackers. The backlash did not fall only on a club that happened to be
German.
Question. If you are asked whether the backlash was fair, whose evidence belongs in the answer —
the burned club, the guarded mosque, Asson, or all of them?




STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
6. Were “all Germans” already interned?
Some later retellings say the German Club stood empty because every German in Australia had
already been interned. That is too strong for 1 January 1915. Internment of “enemy aliens” happened
during the war, and it was not a single clean sweep on one day. The club was burned. German
residents were threatened. How many people were in the club that night, and how internment later
widened, should be checked, not assumed.
Question. What happens to a story about backlash if you write, wrongly, that the target building was
already empty of the people it stood for?

7. Sure, maybe, or a guess?
Sure: a picnic train was fired on on 1 January 1915; four people were killed; Gool and Abdullah were
shot dead; the German Club was burned that night; a mosque was guarded. Maybe: the exact
wording of every sentence in the notes; how long the gunfight lasted; how far a later “planted flag”
claim can go. A guess: a single clean motive, or the private thoughts of Alma Cowie. The opener is not
evidence of 1915 feeling, except as a later reader’s.
Question. Write three labels — sure, maybe, guess — against the case question, and say which witness
pushed you toward each one.

pages.text:
Teacher Note
THE BATTLE OF BROKEN HILL, 1915 · YEAR 9 · TEACHER NOTE


This note is for the teacher. It is not a student page.


What’s true about the opener
The typographic page is a constructed Year 10 student notebook, written for this file, in an
angsty voice. It is not a 1915 diary and not the voice of a named historical person. “A girl my
age” is Alma Priscilla Cowie, 17; the opener does not invent her thoughts or last words. Violence
is named, not described in graphic detail. No death photographs are used anywhere in the file.


Curriculum
The brief asked for an accurate AC9HS9 code. There is no AC9HS9. Year 9 History uses
AC9HH9 codes. The lead code is AC9HH9K11: the effects of the First World War on Australian
society. The shooting happened on Australian soil in January 1915, after the Ottoman Empire
had entered the war; the aftermath includes a riot, a burned German Club, and the treatment of
a local Muslim community. AC9HH9K09 (places Australians fought) is not used as the lead,
because this was not a campaign overseas.


Source conflicts, flagged
Alma / Elma Cowie; Alfred Elton / Elvin Millard; 40 trucks / 41 carriages; “some 1200”
picnickers; gunfight of about 40 minutes / almost two hours; varied spellings of Gool Badsha
Mahomed (Gool, Goul, Mahomed, Mohammed, Mahommed). Translations of the notes do not
all match. Later “planted flag” / forged letter claims are not treated as agreed. Overstatements
that “every German” had already been interned are flagged. Shaw worked in the sanitary
department; the man named in Abdullah’s note is Inspector Brosnan, not Shaw.


Religion, race, and care
Gool and Abdullah were Muslim. The local cameleer community was not the same as the two
men. Teach the faith, and the camp, with respect. Do not let the word “Turk,” which 1915 papers
used because of the flag, erase that uncertainty. Living families, including descendants of
victims and of the camel camp, deserve legal and ethical care even though the principals are
long dead. Year 9–10 students can hold two things at once: the killing of civilians was a crime,
and a riot against other people’s club, camp and mosque still has to be judged.


Country
Broken Hill is on Wilyakali Country. This file does not tell a First Nations history of the event,
and does not invent one. A deeper local treatment would need consultation. The student pages
do not pretend otherwise.

IMAGINED Written for this case, based on real events, not a real document.
                                                                     Somewhere in Australia
               May 1915 · a reconstruction · not a historical document
A newspaper arrives with a long cable from an English
correspondent. It says Australian and New Zealand soldiers have
landed on a beach in Turkey, and are fighting hard. Most people
have never heard of the place.
Within weeks the name “Anzac” is in every paper.
Years later some people will say the nation was born on that
beach. Others will say the nation was already there, and that
what happened later — the long lists of the dead, the two votes
that said “no” to forcing men overseas, and the arguments about
what the day means — matter just as much.
(The opening scene is a reconstruction. The cable and the later
arguments are from the records. See Teacher Note.)

pages.text:
A NOTE BEFORE YOU READ
  This case is about a war in which more than 60,000 Australians died, and many more people of other
  nations. It talks about the dead, about families who argued bitterly, and about words that were meant
  to hurt. Some students will have family names on a local memorial. Take it slowly. No photographs of
  the dead are used. A note for teachers is at the end of the case.




THE ANZAC STORY, 1915–1917 · YEAR 9 · READ
The Anzac Story: Gallipoli, the Legend and the
Conscription Votes
What do the records show about Gallipoli and the conscription votes, and what
can they not settle?


What is agreed
Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber, used in Super Sleuths, marks what is still disputed or was
added later.


  On 25 April 1915 Australian and New Zealand troops landed at what became Anzac Cove, on the
  Gallipoli peninsula in the Ottoman Empire (now Türkiye). It was part of a British-led Allied
  campaign to open the Dardanelles. British troops landed at Cape Helles, further south, the same
  day (Australian War Memorial).




  “Anzac” comes from the initials of the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps, formed in
  Egypt. Clerks at corps headquarters in Cairo shortened the name to a code word. Charles Bean
  credited Lieutenant A. T. White with suggesting “ANZAC.” One of its earliest uses in an official
  document is dated 24 April 1915. After the landing, General Birdwood asked that the beach be
  named Anzac Cove (Australian War Memorial).




  The first detailed account of the landing to reach Australia was by the English correspondent
  Ellis Ashmead-Bartlett. Australian newspapers printed it on 8 May 1915. Charles Bean,
  Australia’s official correspondent, landed on 25 April, but his report was not published in
  Australia until 13 May (Anzac Portal; Sydney Morning Herald, 8 May 1915).




  Anzac and Suvla were evacuated between 15 and 20 December 1915; the last party left Anzac in
  the early hours of 20 December. British and French troops stayed at Helles until 9 January 1916

pages.alt: Page 155. The Anzac Story: Gallipoli. (Anzac Portal). The Australian War Memorial’s accepted official estimate is that 8,709 Australians died at Gallipoli. Far more died on the Western Front in France and Belgium, from 1916 to 1918: more
pages.text:
(Anzac Portal).




The Australian War Memorial’s accepted official estimate is that 8,709 Australians died at
Gallipoli. Far more died on the Western Front in France and Belgium, from 1916 to 1918: more
than 295,000 Australians served there, and over 46,000 died (Department of Veterans’ Affairs).
More than 60,000 Australians died in the war.




Charles Bean’s 286 diaries, notebooks and research folders are now at the Australian War
Memorial (AWM38, 3DRL 606). He edited the Official History of Australia in the War of 1914–
18, twelve volumes published from 1921 to 1942, and wrote six of them himself (Australian War
Memorial).




Prime Minister Billy Hughes asked voters twice to approve conscription for service overseas.
The votes were called referendums at the time, but they were plebiscites: they did not change the
Constitution (Australian War Memorial; Australian Electoral Commission). On 28 October 1916:
1,087,557 Yes and 1,160,033 No. On 20 December 1917: 1,015,159 Yes and 1,181,747 No
(National Archives of Australia). Both were defeated, so the Australian Imperial Force stayed a
volunteer force.




The votes split the Labor Party, communities and families. After the 1916 vote Hughes was
expelled from the Labor Party; with 24 of his supporters he joined the Opposition to form the
Nationalist Party (National Museum of Australia). In 1917 the Catholic Archbishop of
Melbourne, Daniel Mannix, was the most prominent opponent of conscription (Australian War
Memorial). Both sides used strong language. In 1917 a mother whose son had been killed was
sent a copy of the anti-conscription leaflet “The Blood Vote” with the words “from your dead
soldier son” written on the back (Australian War Memorial).




After the war a legend grew around Anzac. The Australian War Memorial lists the qualities
usually linked to it: endurance, courage, ingenuity, good humour and mateship. Historians call
this the Anzac legend, or, more critically, the Anzac myth. Later critics have said that it centred
on white, British-Australian men, and said little about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
soldiers, about women, about the Western Front, or about the divisions at home.

pages.text:
Three witnesses
THE ANZAC STORY, 1915–1917 · YEAR 9 · ASK


Each witness is a real person, or a real set of words from the record. A period portrait is used
where one exists and is free to reuse. Otherwise you will see a plain silhouette, not a likeness.
Ask the same three questions of each.

                                   Charles Bean
                                   Official war correspondent, 1914–1919 · official historian, 1919–1942 · his
                                   notebooks and the Official History

                                   He went ashore on the morning of the landing and kept notebooks for the
                                   rest of the war.
                                   What they said
                                   In his diary in September 1915 he wrote of Ashmead-Bartlett’s reports: “His
                                   written dispatches are full of life and colour, hit hard, and give a brilliant
  A silhouette, not a likeness.
                                   idea which is remarkably true. He exaggerates a bit to make his points …
                                   and yet he’s a lover of the truth.” Thirty years later, describing the
                                   evacuation, he wrote: “Anzac stood, and still stands, for reckless valour in a
                                   good cause, for enterprise, resourcefulness, fidelity, comradeship, and
                                   endurance that will never own defeat.”
                                   Could they have seen it?
                                   Yes, for much of it. The Australian War Memorial says he landed at about
                                   9.20 am on 25 April, and his notebooks record interviews, maps and
                                   sketches made at the time. But no one person saw a whole battle, and his
                                   history was written years later, from his notes, from other men’s accounts
                                   and from official records. The 1946 words are a judgment, not an
                                   observation.
                                   Why might they say it?
                                   He was the official correspondent, writing under censorship, and later the
                                   official historian. He admired the men and wanted their story told truly. He
                                   also helped to shape how Australians remembered the war. Ask how a
                                   notebook from 1915 and a book from 1946 might differ.
                                   Source. C. E. W. Bean, diary, 26 September 1915, AWM38 3DRL 606, Australian War
                                   Memorial, as quoted by the Department of Veterans’ Affairs’ Anzac Portal (“Ellis Ashmead-
                                   Bartlett”). C. E. W. Bean, Anzac to Amiens (1946), as quoted by the Australian War Memorial
                                   (“Anzac spirit”). Bean’s landing time: Australian War Memorial, “A difficult landing.” These
                                   are his recorded words.

                                 Military Service Referendum ballot papers and results · 28 October 1916 and 20
                                 December 1917

                                 Here the witness is the record itself: the question voters were asked, and

                                 What they said
                                 1916: “Are you in favour of the Government having, in this grave
                                 emergency, the same compulsory powers over citizens in regard to
A document silhouette, not a
                                 requiring their military service, for the term of this War, outside the
facsimile. The witness is the    Commonwealth, as it now has in regard to military service within the
           record.               Commonwealth?” Yes 1,087,557; No 1,160,033. Victoria, Western Australia,
                                 Tasmania and the Federal Territories voted Yes. 1917: “Are you in favour of
                                 the proposal of the Commonwealth Government for reinforcing the
                                 Australian Imperial Force overseas?” Yes 1,015,159; No 1,181,747. Only
                                 Western Australia, Tasmania and the Federal Territories voted Yes.
                                 Could they have seen it?
                                 A count can show how many people voted each way, and where. It cannot
                                 show why. It does not record who voted, or what they were afraid of, or how
                                 families argued at the kitchen table.
                                 Why might they say it?
                                 Officials counted the votes to report a result, not to make an argument. But
                                 the questions were written by the government that wanted a Yes, and the
                                 wording changed between the two votes. Ask why.

The three witness cards are Charles Bean, the ballot papers and official results, and the leaflet “The Blood Vote.”

There is no answer at the back. The opening scene is a reconstruction. The landing, the dates,
the counts and the words on the leaflet are from the records. Write one sentence on what the

What do the records show about Gallipoli and the conscription votes, and
what can they not settle?

  MY FINDING
  My finding. ________________________________________________

  What I still can’t know. ___________________________________

Why it still matters
Anzac Day is still the biggest day of remembrance in Australia, and people still argue about
what it means. The conscription votes were two of the few times Australians were asked directly
whether to send men to war, and both times the answer was no. Asking what the records can
prove is a way of asking who gets remembered, and who gets left out.

THE ANZAC STORY, 1915–1917 · YEAR 9 · SUPER SLEUTHS
Super Sleuths
Go further only if you want to. Amber marks what is still disputed, or what later writers added.
Work on paper. Each investigation names the records, or the kind of record, to look for.


  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  1. Legend or myth?
  Some writers call Anzac a “legend,” and some a “myth.” Find one source from the time, such as
  Ashmead-Bartlett’s report in the Sydney Morning Herald of 8 May 1915, or a page of Bean’s
  notebooks on the Australian War Memorial’s website, and one later historian who questions part of
  the story, such as Marilyn Lake and Henry Reynolds, What’s Wrong with Anzac? (2010). Ashmead-
  Bartlett placed the landing at “Gaba Tepe”; the boats actually came ashore further north. Bean said
  his dispatches “exaggerate a bit.”
  Question. Compare their claims. What does each one say happened, and what does each one say it
  means?




  WHAT THE RECORDS SHOW
  2. Evidence for: what the 1915–1918 records show
  1. The date and place of the landing, and the evacuation in December 1915, in unit war diaries and
  Bean’s notebooks. 2. The number of Australian dead, from official casualty returns (8,709 at
  Gallipoli; over 46,000 on the Western Front). 3. The two vote counts, and the questions on the ballot
  papers, in the National Archives.
  Question. Which of these could you check yourself, and where?




  WHAT THE RECORDS DO NOT SHOW
  3. Evidence against: what the records do not show
  1. Whether Australia was “born” at Gallipoli: that is an interpretation, not a fact in any record. 2. Why
  each person voted Yes or No: the count records numbers, not reasons. 3. How many Aboriginal and
  Torres Strait Islander men served: enlistment forms did not record it, and the Memorial says more
  than 1,000, an estimate.
  Question. Why might a gap in the records matter as much as what is in them?

pages.text:
Teacher Note
THE ANZAC STORY, 1915–1917 · YEAR 9 · TEACHER NOTE


This note is for the teacher. It is not a student page.


What’s true about the opener
This note is not part of the student page. The opening scene is a reconstruction and carries an
Imagined badge. No particular newspaper or reader is meant. What is true behind it:
Australians knew by the end of April 1915 that troops had landed, and the first detailed account,
Ellis Ashmead-Bartlett’s, was printed in Australian papers on 8 May 1915 (Sydney Morning
Herald, p. 13; Anzac Portal). The facts on the student pages are from the Australian War
Memorial, the National Museum of Australia, the National Archives of Australia and the
Australian Electoral Commission.


Care this case needs
Some students will have family names on a memorial, or family who argued about conscription,
or who came from countries that fought on the other side. The meaning of Anzac is left open: do
not ask students to decide that the legend is true or false, and do not use role-play of the dead or
of soldiers at the landing. The “from your dead soldier son” message is quoted because the
Australian War Memorial uses it to show how cruel the 1917 campaign became; handle it with
care.


First Nations service
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander service in the First World War was recorded incompletely.
Enlistment forms did not ask for it, and many men hid or were not asked about their heritage,
so numbers are approximate: the Australian War Memorial says more than 1,000. No
individual First Nations soldier is named or pictured in this file. If you add local stories, follow
local protocols and the AIATSIS Code of Ethics.


Source conflicts, flagged
Gallipoli deaths: 8,709 is the accepted official estimate (AWM, from a revised return dated 26
January 1919); the same source’s month-by-month table adds up to 8,159. The 1917 question:
the Parliamentary Handbook and the Australian War Memorial give “reinforcing the Australian
Imperial Force overseas”; the National Archives fact sheet gives “reinforcing the
Commonwealth Forces overseas.” The student page uses the Handbook’s wording. Bean’s
famous “Anzac stood, and still stands” is from Anzac to Amiens (1946), not his wartime
notebooks; the Australian War Memorial calls it widely misquoted. “The Blood Vote” is
catalogued by the Memorial as a leaflet, not a poster. Total war deaths: 61,522 (AWM fatalities
page) or about 60,000 (National Museum of Australia).

Curriculum
Australian Curriculum v9, Year 9 History, World War I (1914–1918): AC9HH9K08 (causes and
reasons for enlisting), AC9HH9K09 (places where Australians fought, including Gallipoli and
the Western Front), AC9HH9K10 (significant events and the nature of warfare), AC9HH9K11
(effects on Australian society, including the conscription debates), and AC9HH9K12
(commemoration and debates about the Anzac legend).

Placement

In this chronological book the case is placed by the landing of 25 April 1915. It follows the Battle
of Broken Hill (1 January 1915) and comes before the hospital ship Centaur (1943). In a
teaching sequence it fits after the causes of the war, and before or alongside the Western Front.

Pictures

Charles Bean is shown as a plain silhouette with a name card. The ballot papers and “The Blood
Vote” are document silhouettes, not facsimiles; the leaflet itself is out of copyright and can be
viewed at the Australian War Memorial (RC00337). No photographs of soldiers or of the dead
are used.

pages.text:
A NOTE BEFORE YOU READ
  This file is about a hospital ship sunk in wartime, with heavy loss of life. It includes named dead,
  injured survivors, and a disputed attribution. Teach it with care for the dead and for their families.
  The opening scene is written for this file; what’s true sits in the teacher notes. A note for teachers is at
  the end of the case.




SISTER ELLEN SAVAGE AND THE HOSPITAL SHIP CENTAUR, 1943 · YEAR 10 ·
READ
Sister Ellen Savage and the hospital ship Centaur,
1943
What can the records prove about who sank a marked hospital ship, and
whether it was legitimately protected?


What is agreed
Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber, used in Super Sleuths, marks what is still disputed or was
added later.


  On 14 May 1943, shortly after 4 a.m., the 2/3rd Australian Hospital Ship Centaur was sunk off
  the Queensland coast. She had left Sydney unescorted on 12 May, bound north, carrying her
  crew and medical staff, including members of the 2/12th Field Ambulance, and no patients. The
  Australian War Memorial places the sinking south of Moreton Island; an older Memorial
  encyclopedia entry gave a position of about 27°17′ S, 153°58′ E, about 50 miles east-north-east
  of Brisbane. Some later accounts give the time as 4.10 a.m. This file uses the Memorial’s
  wording, “shortly after 4 am,” and notes the variation.




  A contemporary correction, reported on 20 May 1943, said that a further check by Australian
  Army and Navy authorities had revised an earlier figure of 363 people on board down to 332,
  “with a corresponding diminution in casualties.” The Australian War Memorial uses the figures
  332 on board and 64 survivors (268 people died). Some later summaries give 322 on board. This
  file uses the Memorial’s 332 and 64, and records that later figures sometimes differ. Twelve
  nursing sisters were on board. Only Sister Ellen Savage, Australian Army Nursing Service,
  survived.




  Period photographs, including Australian War Memorial 302796, a port-side view taken in
  Sydney in 1943 and now in the public domain, show a white hull, a green band, and prominent
  red crosses on the hull, the funnel, and the stern, with another cross lying horizontally on the

pages.alt: Page 173. The hospital ship Centaur. after deckhouse. The Memorial has described the ship as appropriately lit and marked as a hospital ship. One Memorial exhibition page calls her “brightly-lit” at the time she was hit. A photograph of
pages.text:
after deckhouse. The Memorial has described the ship as appropriately lit and marked as a
hospital ship. One Memorial exhibition page calls her “brightly-lit” at the time she was hit. A
photograph of the ship in harbour, and a later official wording about lights, do not by themselves
prove what a submarine commander could see at night.




The sinking was very rapid. One Memorial article says the ship sank in about three minutes.
Some survivors, quoted in a 20 May 1943 newspaper report, said ballast in her bottom helped to
send her under “in a few seconds.” Seaman Martin Pash, as quoted by the Australian War
Memorial, said the Centaur “just went straight down.” The 64 survivors spent about a day and a
half in the water and on rafts before they were spotted by a RAAF aircraft and taken off by the
United States destroyer USS Mugford, as recorded by the Memorial.




Sister Ellen Savage, service number NFX.76584, was the only nurse to survive. The London
Gazette of 25 August 1944 recorded the award of the George Medal to “Sister (Miss) Ellen
Savage, NFX.76584, Australian Army Nursing Service,” “in recognition of conspicuous gallantry
in carrying out hazardous work in a very brave manner.” Two days after the rescue she was
interviewed in hospital by Mervyn Weston; that interview was printed in the Newcastle Morning
Herald and Miners’ Advocate, 19 May 1943, p. 2. The paper called her Eleanor; other reports
used Nellie. The Gazette names her Ellen Savage.




The Australian Government sent an official protest to Japan through Switzerland. The Advocate
(Burnie), 20 May 1943, reported that Prime Minister John Curtin “stated emphatically” that all
those on board were non-combatants, “members of a medical corps,” and that the Army legal
branch held the protection of Army medical personnel on a hospital ship was “clearly expressed
in the Geneva and Hague conventions,” and was not lost because there were no sick or wounded
on board. The Australian War Memorial later summarised that Japan “did not acknowledge
responsibility for the incident for many years,” and that “the War Crimes Tribunal could not
identify the responsible submarine.” A later Japanese official war history, as summarised by the
Memorial, attributed the sinking to submarine I-177 under Lieutenant Commander Nakagawa.
This file records both summaries, and does not treat the later official history as a courtroom
finding.

pages.text:
Sister Ellen Savage, AANS
                              The only nursing sister to survive · Interviewed two days after the rescue ·
                              Awarded the George Medal

                              A named survivor, speaking in hospital in May 1943, about the explosion,
                              her friend, the water, and the raft.
                              What they said
                              Savage said her best friend, Sister King, was in the next cabin, and that she
                              heard her shout, “Quick, Savage, up on deck.” They had often talked about
Sister Ellen Savage, AANS,
                              what they would do if they were ever torpedoed. Sister King could not
Greenslopes Army Hospital,    swim, “and it had been agreed that I should crocodile her — that is, take her
 May 1943. AWM 044428.        across my shoulders — if we ever finished in the water.” “So, after meeting
Copyright expired — public
                              on deck, we jumped into the water together. Sister King was apparently
          domain.
                              killed by debris, for I never saw her again. It was then that I apparently
                              injured my side, but I did not realise it at the time. I am a strong swimmer,
                              and immediately struck away from the ship when I realised that Sister King
                              had disappeared.” She said she climbed onto a section of the deck-house
                              with Robert Westwood, “the 15-year-old cabin boy, who had burns,” and
                              that they worked their way to two rafts “on which nearly 20 men were
                              huddling.” A man gave her a greatcoat. “I gave Westwood what attention I
                              could, and sheltered him against me with the greatcoat. This great coat
                              undoubtedly saved my life.”
                              Could they have seen it?
                              She was on the ship when it was hit, and in the water afterwards. She could
                              speak about what she heard, what she did, and whom she could no longer
                              find. She could not see who fired the torpedo, or from which submarine, or
                              what that person could see of the markings and the lights. She was injured,
                              newly rescued, and speaking to a reporter. A newspaper interview is still a
                              reporter’s wording of what she said. Accounts of her injuries are not
                              identical across the 19 May article and later Memorial quotations.
                              Why might they say it?
                              She was asked, two days after the rescue, to say what had happened. She
                              named her friend, the plan they had made, a boy she tried to help, and a
                              coat that kept her alive. That is evidence of the sinking as a person lived it.
                              It is not evidence of who fired, or of whether the ship’s markings could be
                              seen from a submarine at night.

                               Could they have seen it?
                               The camera, in Sydney harbour in 1943, could record how the ship was
                               painted. It could not record how those markings looked from a submarine
                               at sea, shortly after four in the morning, off the Queensland coast. An
                               official description that the ship was lit and marked is strong evidence of
                               how the Allies presented her. It is not, by itself, proof of what the person
                               who fired could see, or of whether a notification of her identity — if one was
                               sent, and if it arrived — had been read. Some later official and education
                               accounts say her identification was passed to the International Committee
                               of the Red Cross and to Japan in early February 1943. This file has not
                               inspected the original notification papers, and does not treat that date as
                               proved here.
                               Why might they say it?
                               Hospital ships were painted and lit so that, under the conventions, they
                               could be recognised and left alone. After the sinking, official Australian
                               voices had a reason to stress those markings, the lights, and the legal
                               protection. That does not make the photograph untrue. It does mean
                               students should ask what the markings can prove, and what they cannot.
                               Source. Australian War Memorial 302796, “Port side view of the hospital ship Centaur,”
                               Sydney, 1943. The Memorial’s caption notes the red crosses and green lines on the hull,
                               funnel, stern, and after deckhouse. Copyright expired — public domain. Official wording on
                               lighting and marking is from the Australian War Memorial, including an exhibition page
                               that calls the ship “brightly-lit” when she was hit. The Advocate (Burnie), 20 May 1943,
                               records the Army legal branch on the Geneva and Hague conventions.

SISTER ELLEN SAVAGE AND THE HOSPITAL SHIP CENTAUR, 1943 ·

My finding
YEAR 10 · DECIDE

The three witness cards are Sister Ellen Savage, the hospital ship Centaur as marked, and the official Japanese
record (including the later naming of I-177 and Lieutenant Commander Hajime Nakagawa).

There is no answer at the back. The narrator of the notebook is invented. The quotations, the
1943 photographs, the Gazette award, and the official summaries are not. Write only what these
records can support. One of the findings you may choose is that we can’t know.

What can the records prove about who sank a marked hospital ship, and
whether it was legitimately protected?
Circle one: The records show a marked, and officially described as lit, hospital ship was sunk, and 268
people died · The records can prove the markings in the 1943 photograph, but not what a submarine
commander could see at night · The records can prove an official Australian protest, and that Japan
did not then accept responsibility · A later official Japanese war history, as summarised by the
Memorial, names I-177 and Nakagawa, but that is not the same as a courtroom finding · We can’t
know, from this file, who fired, or whether the person who fired could see that she was a hospital ship ·
Another finding, written below


  MY FINDING
  My finding. ________________________________________________
  ______________________________________________________________
  The one piece of evidence that most changed my mind. ________
  ______________________________________________________________
  What I still can’t know. ___________________________________
  ______________________________________________________________




Why it still matters
Hospital ships, and the rules meant to protect them, are still argued over when a marked ship is
hit. The Centaur is commemorated in Australia as an atrocity; the question of who fired, and of
what could be seen, has never been settled in a court. Families of the dead, and the wreck itself
— found in 2009 and protected as a historic shipwreck and a memorial — are not a puzzle for
students to solve. A careful finding will say what the 1943 records and the later official
summaries can show, and what they cannot.

  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  1. What could be seen at night?
  Allied official sources, including the Australian War Memorial, describe the Centaur as clearly
  marked and brightly lit. The 1943 photograph in this file shows the markings in harbour, in daylight.
  A submarine at periscope depth, shortly after 4 a.m., is a different point of view. Some later official
  and education accounts say her identification was passed to the International Committee of the Red
  Cross and to Japan in early February 1943. This file has not inspected those notification papers. A
  notification, even if it was sent and received, is not the same as a commander seeing a red cross in the
  dark.
  Question. What can a photograph of a marked ship, an official wording about lights, and a claimed
  notification, each prove — and what can none of them prove about the view from a submarine?




  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  2. Who fired? The closed file and the later history
  The Memorial’s encyclopedia entry records that post-war investigators could not identify the
  responsible submarine, and that a later Japanese official war history attributed the sinking to I-177
  under Lieutenant Commander Hajime Nakagawa. Nakagawa did not comment on the Centaur. He
  was convicted of other war crimes, for firing on survivors of another ship, not for this one. Some later
  naval histories have pointed to other Japanese submarines then off the east coast, and have not all
  agreed on I-177. This file does not treat the 1979 history, as reported by the Memorial, as a courtroom
  finding, and it does not invent a confession.
  Question. If a later official history names a submarine, and a completed prosecution never did, what
  should a careful finding say?




  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  3. Cargo, rifles, and the conventions
  After the sinking, and in later education materials, claims have been made about weapons and cargo:




                           Reopen the Record: Australian Histories · sample ·   179

pages.alt: Page 180. The hospital ship Centaur. that ambulance drivers tried to bring rifles and ammunition aboard; that the Master and the Chief Medical Officer questioned what the conventions allowed; that a search was made; that figures of
pages.text:
that ambulance drivers tried to bring rifles and ammunition aboard; that the Master and the Chief
Medical Officer questioned what the conventions allowed; that a search was made; that figures of
about 52 rifles and 2,000 or 4,000 rounds appear in later retellings. Those figures do not all match,
even in the same later materials. The Hague conventions allowed some arms for the maintenance of
order and the defence of the wounded. The Memorial’s main accounts of the sinking emphasise the
markings, the lights, and the loss of life, not a cargo of munitions. This file does not settle how many
rifles, if any, were in a hold, and it does not use an unsettled cargo claim to decide whether the ship
was legitimately protected.
Question. Why might later writers argue about cargo and rifles, and why should a student keep those
claims in amber until a named primary source is on the desk?




STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
4. Numbers that moved
In the week after the sinking, a reported official correction revised 363 people on board down to 332.
The Memorial uses 332 and 64 survivors. Some later pages say 322. Figures for the 2/12th Field
Ambulance also vary between later captions and later articles (for example, 14 survivors from “two
hundred,” or 178 dead from 193). This file uses the Memorial’s 332 and 64, and the correction
reported on 20 May 1943, and leaves the smaller disagreements in amber.
Question. Why might official numbers change in the first week, and why does a later disagreement
about a unit total not undo the fact of the sinking?




STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
5. The wreck is a memorial, not a hunt
The wreck was found on 20 December 2009, about 30 nautical miles off the southern tip of Moreton
Island, in deep water, and is now a protected historic shipwreck and a memorial. That discovery is
part of the later history of the case. It is not the student question, and the site is not to be treated as a
puzzle or a treasure hunt.
Question. Why might finding the wreck still leave the question of who fired, and of what could be
seen, unsettled?

SISTER ELLEN SAVAGE AND THE HOSPITAL SHIP CENTAUR, 1943 · YEAR 10 ·

Teacher Note
TEACHER NOTE


This note is for the teacher. It is not a student page.


What’s true about the opener
The narrator is an invented present-day journalist, not a real person, and is not based on a
named reporter. The journalist is shown looking through four artefacts before deciding to
reopen the case. The journalist’s thoughts refer only to what those artefacts show. They do not
invent historical facts, last words, or quotations. The picture at the start of the opening scene is
a real photograph: the starboard bow of the hospital ship Centaur in Sydney in 1943, Australian
War Memorial 302800 (photographer not identified; copyright expired, public domain). It
replaces an earlier AI-generated illustration. The photograph is real; the journalist and the desk
scene around it are invented, which is why the page carries an Imagined badge. The quoted
words that appear after the newspaper extract — “My best friend, Sister King, was in the next
cabin” and “Quick, Savage, up on deck” — are from the Newcastle Morning Herald and Miners’
Advocate, 19 May 1943, p. 2. Curtin’s “stated emphatically,” “non-combatants,” and “members
of a medical corps,” and the Army legal branch wording about the Geneva and Hague
conventions, are from the reconstructed bulletin, which takes every sentence from the Advocate
(Burnie), 20 May 1943, p. 3. The photograph and its verso caption are AWM 302796. The
telegram is a labelled reconstruction, not a real telegram, and is not addressed to a real family.
The Memorial’s wording about lights, the figures 332 and 64, Seaman Martin Pash’s phrase
“just went straight down,” and the later conflict over I-177 sit in the case file, not in the opening
scene; they are not invented. Sister King is named because Savage named her in the published
1943 interview. Teach that name with care for the dead and for families.


What’s true about the exhibits
Four exhibits sit inside the opening scene, with the journalist’s reactions between them. The
casualty telegram is a reconstruction, clearly labelled, and is not a real telegram. It is addressed
only to “the next of kin of a nursing sister,” not to a named family. The wording is modelled on
official Army casualty telegrams of the period, including a Postmaster-General’s Department
telegram in the Australian War Memorial’s papers of Reginald Walter Saunders, and the
published military formula that begins “I regret to inform you” and conveys the sympathy of the
Minister for the Army. The photograph is AWM 302796, Sydney, 1943, copyright expired —
public domain. The handwritten caption on the back is the Memorial’s own catalogue wording,
not an invented personal note. The radio bulletin is a reconstruction, not an original script or an
original recording. Every sentence is taken from “Protest against sinking of Centaur,” Advocate
(Burnie), 20 May 1943, p. 3, http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article68810542, including Curtin’s
“stated emphatically,” “non-combatants,” and “members of a medical corps,” and the Army
legal branch’s wording about the Geneva and Hague conventions. The audio in the app is a

names her Eleanor; the London Gazette names her Ellen Savage, NFX.76584.


Sensitivities: war dead, families, and injuries
Two hundred and sixty-eight people died. Teach the sinking with care. Do not use photographs
of human remains, or of bodies in the water, if they exist. Do not invent last words, panic, or
suffering beyond what a named source actually says. Accounts of Savage’s injuries are not
identical; do not tidy them into one medical list. A 15-year-old cabin boy with burns is in the
1943 interview. Handle that line carefully in a Year 10 classroom. The case is not a First Nations
history as a whole, but a contemporary crew-survivor list printed on 20 May 1943 named E. M.
Salt as a “Torres strait pilot.” This file does not examine that person’s story. If you take it
further, do so with care, and with consultation if a Torres Strait Islander’s experience is taught
in any depth.


I-177 and Nakagawa: do not settle a closed prosecution
Present the conflict, do not close it. The Memorial records that the war-crimes process could
not identify the submarine, and that a later Japanese official war history named I-177 and
Lieutenant Commander Hajime Nakagawa. Nakagawa did not comment on the Centaur. He
died in 1991, so he is not a living person, but legal care still applies to how he is named: he was
convicted of other crimes, not tried for this one. Do not print a student-facing finding that treats
him as the settled offender. Some later naval histories have preferred other boats then off the
east coast. If you use later press reports of a Japanese embassy comment after the 2009 wreck
discovery, quote a named article, and do not treat a diplomatic wording as a verdict either way.


Markings, lights, notification, and cargo
Allied official sources say the ship was marked and lit. That is evidence. Students should still
ask what a submarine commander could see, and what a claimed notification to Japan can
actually prove. This file has not inspected original ICRC or Japanese notification papers, and so
does not treat a February 1943 notification date as agreed fact. Cargo and rifle claims belong in
Super Sleuths. Figures in later education materials conflict. Do not use an unsettled munitions
story to decide the legal protection of a hospital ship, and do not invent a hidden cargo.


Names, numbers, and sources not used
1943 newspapers used Eleanor and Nellie as well as Ellen; the Gazette and the Memorial use
Ellen Savage, NFX.76584. An early official total of 363 was corrected to 332 in May 1943. Prefer
the Memorial’s 332 and 64, and flag later 322s. The AWM newsreel F00734, in which Savage
was interviewed from a hospital bed, is not treated as public domain and is not used as a still in
this file. A longer wording sometimes circulated as her George Medal “citation” has not been

Curriculum, placement, and publishing
This file is for Year 10, AC9HH10K02: “the places where Australians fought, and their
perspectives and experiences during the Second World War, such as the fall of Singapore,
prisoners of war (POWs), the Battle of Britain and Kokoda.” Whether that code is the best fit is
still a teacher’s judgement; the official examples on the v9 page do not name the Centaur, but
the case is a documented Australian experience of the war at sea, off the Queensland coast. The
wreck is mentioned for the teacher and in Super Sleuths, not as the student hunt. Pictures:
Savage and the ship are public-domain Memorial photographs, each captioned with their
accession numbers. The third image is a silhouette, labelled as a silhouette, not a likeness.

Students can also read the notebook as an interactive book, on a tablet or phone. The page

pages.text:
IMAGINED Written for this case, based on real events, not a real document.

                                                                                    20 February 1965
                                                                                              Moree

Egg on my sleeve. I keep wiping it. Still there.

We came back. We had to. Last time they said the ban was off. We left. They put it
back on. I don’t know why I thought a meeting would be enough.

The crowd was already at the pool. Pressing in. So hot I could hardly breathe.
Someone spat. Then the tomatoes, the eggs. I have never been looked at like that.

I keep thinking we don’t live here. We’re from Sydney. We get on the bus. The
children don’t.

The police said if we stayed it would get worse. We stayed. I wanted to go. I hate
that I wanted to go.

Charlie wouldn’t move from the gate. They grabbed him. For a moment I couldn’t see
the kids and I thought —

I thought I would be braver than this.

One of the children was knocked down. They were frightened. So was I. What a thing
to come all this way and still be frightened.

They let them in, in the end. We went in too. For a minute it felt like winning. Then
we had to walk to the bus in a single line and they were still throwing things and
the windows kept getting hit.

A man at the bus said it quietly.

They’ll wait till you’re gone.                  IMAGINED

                                                                                       — on the bus
