THE FREEDOM RIDE · YEAR 10 · READ
What happened in the towns the students visited,
and who recorded it?
The Freedom Ride · New South Wales, February 1965
This investigation acknowledges Aboriginal communities of the towns visited, especially Moree and
Walgett, and those they name. It uses published records, with AIATSIS guidance.
Read the notebook page through to the last line. Then read what the 1965 file can agree on. After
that, three people will be asked the same three questions.

  CASE FILE: FREEDOM RIDE / 1965
  Date of incident      12–26 February 1965 (Moree visits: 16 and 19–20 February)
  Location          Regional New South Wales, including Walgett and Moree
  Status             Unresolved contradictions
  Key claims still disputed
  – What actually changed in the towns, and for how long?
  – Whose record should we trust — student diaries, local Aboriginal accounts, or the 1965
  newspapers and television?
  – When was the Moree baths ban really lifted?




  WHAT IS AGREED · FROM THE 1965 FILE, AND AFTER
  Twenty-nine University of Sydney students left around midnight on 12 February 1965, as Student Action
  for Aborigines (SAFA). Charles Perkins, an Arrernte man, was president. Some left later and others joined.

  They travelled through regional New South Wales for about two weeks, using surveys, pickets and
  cameras, and they kept diaries. Newspapers, radio and television reported the trip as it happened.

  They went to Moree twice. On 16 February, Aboriginal children were at first refused the baths, then let in.
  That evening a public meeting voted 88 to 10 to remove the segregation clause.

  After they left, the old 1955 rule was enforced again. They returned on 19–20 February. A hostile crowd
  met them at the pool. Eggs, tomatoes and stones were thrown. Children and students went in, then left
  that night through the crowd.

  Local Aboriginal people were already campaigning in towns such as Walgett. The students met Harry Hall,
  president of the Walgett Aborigines’ Progressive Association, on 15 February.

  The Moree baths rule used the period language of racial exclusion. The wording is in Super Sleuths, with a
  content note. The ban was not settled in a single day.




Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber, used in Super Sleuths, marks what is still disputed or was
added later.

  Content note. The 1955 Moree baths rule used racist period language. It is quoted here only as a short,

pages.text:
THE FREEDOM RIDE · YEAR 10 · TEACHER NOTE
Teacher note
This investigation acknowledges Aboriginal communities of the towns visited, especially
Moree and Walgett, and those they name. It uses published records, with AIATSIS guidance.


The opener
The notebook is constructed. It is not an original 1965 page, and the handwriting is not original. The
student page carries an Imagined badge, and the closing line is marked Imagined; the detail sits in
this teacher note. The writer is an unnamed city student on the bus, in the spirit of diaries kept on
the trip; the page is not Ann Curthoys’s diary and must not be taught as hers. The date is 20
February 1965, the second Moree visit, after the first meeting and after the ban was put back on.
Scene details — the reimposed ban, the hostile crowd, spit, eggs, tomatoes, stones, the police
warning, Perkins taken from the gate, a child knocked down, frightened children, going in, and
leaving in single file while things were still being thrown — follow Ann Curthoys’s contemporary
diary (AIATSIS collection; published 2002) and Charles Perkins’s later account of the return, as
quoted on the AIATSIS Freedom Ride page. The outline’s “four nights ago,” the 16 February date,
the SAFA title, the method-explaining paragraph, the 88-to-10 vote, the by-law wording, the
number aboard, Gary Williams, and Lismore were taken off this page. They belong in What is
agreed, Super Sleuths, or this note.

Two short conversations in the source outline — a twelve-year-old who had never been inside, and a
woman from the mission — were invented details inside a known sequence. They have been cut.
Two scene lines were checked against the 20 February record and kept. “Charlie wouldn’t move
from the gate. They grabbed him.” Curthoys’s diary of the return, as quoted by AIATSIS, records:
“Charlie started talking to the crowd, but there was a lot of hissing and booing. Then he went to the
front of the line and when he refused to move was grabbed and taken away from the line.” Perkins,
in A Bastard Like Me (1975), also quoted by AIATSIS, places the struggle at the gate: “The mayor
ordered the police to have us removed from the gate entrance. They took hold of my arm and the
struggle started.” The notebook’s “from the gate” is a short compression of those two accounts of the
same confrontation. “One of the children was knocked down.” Curthoys’s diary, as quoted by
AIATSIS, records: “One child had been knocked down. The poor kids were very frightened.” She
wrote that the children told the students this, and that they had also been subjected to racist abuse
(the wording is not repeated on the student pages). Contemporary newspaper headlines of 21–22
February 1965 report a violent confrontation at Moree (among them the Daily Mirror, 21 February,
and the Sydney Morning Herald, 22 February). This file did not independently recover those two
exact phrases from a Trove article body. The closing is now: “A man at the bus said it quietly.” then
“They’ll wait till you’re gone.” Both the speaker and the line are constructed. The man is not a
named historical person. Do not teach either as a documented 1965 quotation. The line stands in for
a documented pattern: after the first Moree visit the ban was reimposed once the bus had left, and
later Moree memory records a similar fear. In 2025, Gomeroi man Uncle Darryl French, who was on
the bus to the pool on the return visit, recalled people saying that when the students left, local
people would have to deal with it (ABC News, 22 February 2025). Living people, including French,
are not given dates on the student pages.




                         Reopen the Record: Australian Histories · sample ·   192

pages.alt: Page 193. The Freedom Ride. Corrections and flags Two Moree visits, not one. The source outline merged them. First visit, Wednesday 16 February 1965: a picket; children at first refused, then let in; an evening public meeting
pages.text:
Corrections and flags
Two Moree visits, not one. The source outline merged them. First visit, Wednesday 16 February
1965: a picket; children at first refused, then let in; an evening public meeting at the Memorial Hall,
initially hostile, at which a motion to remove the segregation clause was carried 88 votes to 10
(Curthoys’s diary, via AIATSIS; also ABC News, 2025). On 17 February, after the students had left,
Aboriginal children tried to get in after school; the mayor then said the 6 June 1955 statute would be
enforced (Curthoys, 18 February entry). In Tenterfield the students voted to return. Second visit,
Saturday 19–Sunday 20 February: a hostile crowd; eggs, tomatoes, stones, spit and scuffles; the
mayor said he would sign a motion to rescind, with conditions; children and students went in; they
left that night in single file (Curthoys’s diary; Perkins, A Bastard Like Me, via AIATSIS; ABC News,
2019 and 2025). Do not teach the ban as settled on 16 February. Curthoys later recalled that it took
about six months before the council formally rescinded the rule (ABC News, 27 September 2019).

Route and Lismore. The students left Sydney around midnight on Friday 12 February. A day-by-
day itinerary published by AIATSIS is: 12 Sydney; 13 Wellington; 14 Gulargambone; 15 Walgett; 16
Moree (first); 17 Boggabilla; 18 Tenterfield, then back; 19–20 Moree (return); 21 Grafton; 22
Lismore and Cabbage Tree Island; 23 Bowraville; 24 Kempsey; 25 Taree; 26 Sydney. They did not
leave for Lismore after the first Moree meeting. Some other lists add towns such as Warwick, Glen
Innes, Inverell or Coffs Harbour; treat those as a minor conflict in the route lists, not a problem to
resolve on the student page.

Numbers aboard. Twenty-nine students left Sydney on 12 February (University of Sydney;
Sydney Barani; AIATSIS). About 35 took part in all, because some left and others joined (AIATSIS).
Keep 29 as the departure figure, and flag that the complement changed.

By-law wording. The outline shortened the rule to “No person being a full-blooded or half-caste
aboriginal… shall use the baths.” ABC News (22 February 2025) quotes a fuller wording, used in
Super Sleuths with a content note. Wording and spelling vary slightly across later accounts; this file
has not checked the 1955 council instrument itself. The statute is often dated 6 June 1955
(Curthoys).

Gary Williams. A Gumbaynggirr-Bundjalung student, and one of two Aboriginal students at the
University of Sydney with Perkins. He was a member of SAFA, but he was not on the bus from
Sydney and he was not at either Moree visit. He was called home for a family emergency and joined
at Bowraville on 23 February, later confining his activism to locations on his own country
(University of Sydney, 2024; NSWALC; Sydney Barani; ABC News, 2025). The outline’s line that he
was “meant to join us later” and would “only come on the stretch that is his own country” over-
explains the delay. He is living: no dates on the student pages. He is named only in Super Sleuths
and this note.

Perkins’s words and graduation. “The problem is out in the open now” is kept, cited from
AIATSIS as said at the 1965 FCAATSI conference in Canberra, to about 200 people. This file has not
independently checked a 1965 conference transcript. The phrase “second class is not good enough”
appears in later interviews and education pages; it has not been pinned here to a 1965 primary
source, and it is not used on the student pages. Do not call Perkins “the first Aboriginal person to
graduate.” He graduated from the University of Sydney in 1966, and is often described as the first
Aboriginal man to do so; Margaret Valadian graduated from the University of Queensland in the



                          Reopen the Record: Australian Histories · sample ·   193

pages.alt: Page 194. The Freedom Ride. same year, and is acknowledged as the first Aboriginal woman to complete an Australian university degree. Valadian is living: no dates on the student pages. The graduation claim is omitted from the
pages.text:
same year, and is acknowledged as the first Aboriginal woman to complete an Australian university
degree. Valadian is living: no dates on the student pages. The graduation claim is omitted from the
student card.

A misattributed quotation. The source outline gave Ann Curthoys the line that the ride
“convinced a very wide section of the public that things were very, very bad.” That wording is Jim
Spigelman’s, in a BBC interview published in 2015, not Curthoys’s. It has been removed from her
card.

The third witness. The source outline used a group card, “Local Aboriginal voices.” This file
names Harry Hall, president of the Walgett Aborigines’ Progressive Association in 1965, because a
documented local Aboriginal person from that year, with a citable role, is a better fit for the three-
witness pattern. He met the students in Walgett; local campaigning was already underway, with
others including Ted Fields; later in 1965 he asked Perkins to return over the colour bar at the Oasis
Hotel (AIATSIS; ABC News, 2025; Walgett AMS Freedom Ride project). The card is lean on
purpose: it is not a 1965 first-person diary, and later family memory (including Amy Townsend’s
account of her grandfather) belongs in discussion, not as if it were written in February 1965. Do not
conflate him with his son, Harry Phillip Hall, who is living, who also assisted in 1965, and who must
not be given dates on a student page. Other later Moree and Bowraville oral histories — including
Wayne Nean and Aunty Sandra Buchanan, both living — are not added as extra cards here.


Pictures, language, and care
The three images are plain mid-century-style silhouettes with name cards, not likenesses of the
people named. No portrait has been invented. A 1965 photograph of Perkins, from the State Library
of New South Wales Tribune set, appears on Wikimedia Commons as Flickr Commons “no known
copyright restrictions,” but the library catalogue also records courtesy of Tribune / SEARCH
Foundation. This file uses a silhouette rather than the photograph. Student pages avoid slur-spelled-
out language and keep violence at the level the diaries record (eggs, tomatoes, stones, spit, shoving,
a child knocked down). Teacher preview is required. Period wording appears only as a short
attributed extract, with a content note.


Cultural care and teaching
Acknowledge the Aboriginal communities of the towns visited in 1965 — especially Moree
(Gamilaraay / Gomeroi) and Walgett (Wayilwan, Gamilaraay and Yuwaalaraay), and the other
communities on the route — and those they name, following AIATSIS guidance. Use the
community’s own names for Country. Local protest did not begin when the bus arrived. Do not let a
Sydney student notebook stand in for a local Aboriginal account. AIATSIS Code of Ethics; guidelines
for ethical publishing; free, prior and informed consent; agreement on what may be quoted. No
sacred or secret material. This investigation uses published, cited records and stays open to
correction.


Curriculum and sources
Year 10, the modern world and Australia: rights and freedoms. AC9HH10K10, the contributions of
significant individuals and groups in the campaign for the recognition of the rights of First Nations

IMAGINED Written for this case, based on real events, not a real document.
                                                    The back page of my exercise book
                      A constructed notebook · not a historical document
Steve’s birthday came out of the barrel. They draw marbles
marked with dates, and if your birthday is drawn, the army can
call you up. Mum said it was like a lottery, except nobody
wanted to win.
He was twenty. Old enough to be called up. Not old enough to
vote. You had to be twenty-one for that.
We had his twenty-first all planned: the church hall, the
streamers, Nan’s sponge with the candles. By then he was in the
army. Then he was in Vietnam.
Dad says we went because South Vietnam asked us to. Miss says
find the letter, and look at the date on it.
We had the party anyway. Nobody sat in his chair.

   He didn’t come home. I still want to know who asked.

pages.text:
A NOTE BEFORE YOU READ
  This case is about a war in which Australians, and many more Vietnamese people, were killed. It talks
  about conscription, a battle and street protests. Families in Australia and in Vietnam still live with
  this history, and some people who were there are still alive. Take it slowly. No photographs of the
  dead are used. A note for teachers is at the end of the case.




VIETNAM AND THE BIRTHDAY BALLOT, 1964–1972 · YEAR 10 · READ
Vietnam and the birthday ballot, 1964–1972
Why did Australia go to Vietnam, and who really asked?


What is agreed
Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber, used in Super Sleuths, marks what is still disputed or was
added later.


  On 5 November 1964 the Menzies Cabinet decided to bring in compulsory, selective national
  service. The National Service Act 1964, passed on 24 November, required 20-year-old men, if
  selected, to serve in the Army for two years of continuous service (cut to eighteen months in
  1971), followed by three years in the Reserve.




  Registration was compulsory for most 20-year-old men. A ballot then chose who would be called
  up. Marbles marked with birth dates were drawn from a lottery barrel, twice a year, and men
  whose birthdays were drawn could be called up. The first ballot was drawn on 10 March 1965.
  Twenty-year-olds could not vote in federal elections: the voting age was then 21.




  In May 1965 the Defence Act was changed so that national servicemen could be made to serve
  overseas. Harold Holt became Prime Minister on 26 January 1966. In March 1966 he announced
  that national servicemen would be sent to Vietnam. On 29 June 1966, on the White House lawn
  in Washington, he told President Lyndon Johnson that Australia would be “all the way with
  LBJ” (PM Transcripts 1339).




  On 17 December 1967 Holt disappeared while swimming at Cheviot Beach, near Portsea in
  Victoria. His body was never found. A Commonwealth and Victoria Police report of January
  1968 found no sign that it was anything other than accidental (National Archives of Australia).
  In 2005 the Victorian State Coroner found that he had drowned.




                            Reopen the Record: Australian Histories · sample ·   199

pages.alt: Page 200. Vietnam and the birthday ballot. Late in the evening of Thursday 29 April 1965, Prime Minister Robert Menzies told the House of Representatives that Australia would send an infantry battalion to South Vietnam, in response to “a reque
pages.text:
Late in the evening of Thursday 29 April 1965, Prime Minister Robert Menzies told the House of
Representatives that Australia would send an infantry battalion to South Vietnam, in response
to “a request from the Government of South Vietnam.” An exchange of letters between
Australia’s Ambassador in Saigon, H. D. Anderson, and South Vietnam’s Prime Minister, Dr
Phan Huy Quat, is dated the same day, 29 April 1965. Prime Minister William McMahon tabled
copies of both letters in Parliament in August 1971.




The government pointed to two treaties. ANZUS (1951) linked Australia, New Zealand and the
United States. SEATO, the South-East Asia Collective Defence Treaty signed at Manila on 8
September 1954, covered South Vietnam through a protocol, but said that no action would be
taken on such a territory “except at the invitation or with the consent of the government
concerned.”




On 18 August 1966, in a rubber plantation at Long Tan in Phuoc Tuy province, 105 men of D
Company, 6th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment, and three New Zealand artillerymen fought
a much larger Viet Cong force for about three hours. The Australian War Memorial records 17
Australians killed and 25 wounded, one of whom died of his wounds days later. Eleven of the
Australian dead were national servicemen. How many Vietnamese soldiers died is disputed (see
Super Sleuths).




On 8 May 1970 the first Vietnam Moratorium asked for two things: bring Australian troops
home, and end conscription. The National Museum of Australia puts the national turnout at
about 200,000. In Melbourne, where Jim Cairns MP led the march, estimates run from about
70,000 to more than 100,000. It was largely peaceful. A second Moratorium on 18 September
1970 was smaller, and there were mass arrests in Sydney and Adelaide. A third followed on 30
June 1971.




The Australian War Memorial says more than 60,000 Australians served in Vietnam from 1962,
and 524 died as a result of the war (the Memorial’s earlier figure was 523: see the Teacher Note).
The last battalion left Nui Dat in November 1971; the last advisers came home in December
1972. That month the new Whitlam government stopped the call-up. Far more Vietnamese
people died than Australians. This file does not try to count them.

pages.alt: Page 201. Vietnam and the birthday ballot. Three witnesses VIETNAM AND THE BIRTHDAY BALLOT, 1964–1972 · YEAR 10 · ASK Each witness is a real person, or a real set of words from the record. A period portrait is used where one exists and is free
pages.text:
Three witnesses
VIETNAM AND THE BIRTHDAY BALLOT, 1964–1972 · YEAR 10 · ASK


Each witness is a real person, or a real set of words from the record. A period portrait is used
where one exists and is free to reuse. Otherwise you will see a plain silhouette, not a likeness.
Ask the same three questions of each.

                                    Robert Menzies
                                    Prime Minister of Australia · statement to the House of Representatives,
                                    Canberra, 29 April 1965

                                    A ministerial statement, made late in the evening, to a half-empty House.
                                    What they said
                                    “The Australian Government is now in receipt of a request from the
                                    Government of South Vietnam for further military assistance.” He also said
                                    that “we decided in principle some time ago—weeks and weeks ago—that
  A silhouette, not a likeness.
                                    we would be willing to do this if we received the necessary request from the
                                    Government of South Vietnam and the necessary collaboration with the
                                    United States.” And: “The takeover of South Vietnam would be a direct
                                    military threat to Australia and all the countries of South and South East
                                    Asia. It must be seen as part of a thrust by Communist China between the
                                    Indian and Pacific Oceans.”
                                    Could they have seen it?
                                    He led the government that made the decision. According to the National
                                    Museum of Australia, word that Quat had agreed reached him only about
                                    three hours before he spoke. He was in Canberra, not in Saigon, when the
                                    letters were exchanged. By his own words, the decision in principle came
                                    weeks before the request.
                                    Why might they say it?
                                    To explain a decision to send soldiers to war, and to show that South
                                    Vietnam wanted them there and that the treaties allowed it. Ask why the
                                    word “request” mattered so much on that night.
                                    Source. Commonwealth Parliamentary Debates, House of Representatives, 29 April 1965,
                                    vol. 45, pp. 1060–1. Text checked against the Hansard print held by PM Transcripts
                                    (transcript 1105). These are his recorded words.

                                    What did they say they saw? · Could they really have seen it? · Why might they say it?

pages.alt: Page 202. Vietnam and the birthday ballot. Dr Phan Huy Quat Prime Minister of the Republic of Vietnam (South Vietnam) · letter to the Australian Ambassador, Saigon, 29 April 1965 A short reply to a letter the Ambassador, H. D. Anderson, wrote
pages.text:
Dr Phan Huy Quat
                                  Prime Minister of the Republic of Vietnam (South Vietnam) · letter to the
                                  Australian Ambassador, Saigon, 29 April 1965

                                  A short reply to a letter the Ambassador, H. D. Anderson, wrote the same
                                  day.
                                  What they said
                                  Quat referred to the Ambassador’s letter “of today’s date confirming the
                                  Australian Government’s offer to send to Viet Nam an infantry battalion of
A document silhouette, not a
                                  800 men.” He wrote: “I wish to confirm my government’s acceptance of
facsimile. The witness is the     this offer and to request the dispatch of this force to Viet Nam on the basis
            letter.               which we discussed.”
                                  Could they have seen it?
                                  He was the head of the government that was “asking,” and he knew what
                                  had been said in the room. But his letter answers an offer. It does not say
                                  who raised the idea first, or how hard he was pressed to agree.
                                  Why might they say it?
                                  Under SEATO, action on South Vietnam’s territory needed his
                                  government’s invitation or consent. Saying yes kept powerful allies close.
                                  We do not have his private reasons, and this file does not invent them.
                                  Source. Letters of 29 April 1965, H. D. Anderson to Phan Huy Quat, and Phan Huy Quat to
                                  H. D. Anderson (No 511-TTP/VP/M), tabled in the House of Representatives by Prime
                                  Minister William McMahon in August 1971. Text from PM Transcripts, transcript 2459
                                  (press release of 19 August 1971).

                                  What did they say they saw? · Could they really have seen it? · Why might they say it?

pages.alt: Page 203. Vietnam and the birthday ballot. Arthur Calwell Leader of the Opposition · reply in the House of Representatives, 4 May 1965 His reply, five days after the announcement. He had already left Canberra when Menzies spoke. What they said
pages.text:
Arthur Calwell
                                  Leader of the Opposition · reply in the House of Representatives, 4 May 1965

                                  His reply, five days after the announcement. He had already left Canberra
                                  when Menzies spoke.
                                  What they said
                                  He said that “even two hours before the Prime Minister rose to make his
                                  statement it was being said on his behalf that there was no certainty that
                                  any statement would be made at all.” Then: “we oppose the Government’s
A silhouette, not a likeness.     decision to send 800 men to fight in Vietnam. We oppose it firmly and
                                  completely.” “We do not think it is a wise decision. We do not think it is a
                                  timely decision.” He said it would “prolong and deepen the suffering of that
                                  unhappy people so that Australia’s very name may become a term of
                                  reproach among them.”
                                  Could they have seen it?
                                  He was not in Cabinet, and he had not seen the cables or the letters. He was
                                  reacting to the decision, not watching it being made. He knew how the
                                  announcement had been handled in Parliament.
                                  Why might they say it?
                                  He led a party that opposed sending the battalion, and he believed the
                                  decision would harm Australia’s security. He was also arguing against the
                                  government in Parliament, so his words were part of a political contest as
                                  well.
                                  Source. Commonwealth Parliamentary Debates, House of Representatives, 4 May 1965, vol.
                                  46, pp. 1102–7, as cited in a classroom source pack by the ANZAC Day Commemoration

My finding
DECIDE

The three witness cards are Robert Menzies, Dr Phan Huy Quat speaking through his letter, and Arthur Calwell.

There is no answer at the back. Steve and the notebook are invented. The letters, the speeches
and the dates are not. Write only what these records can support. One of the findings you may
choose is that we can’t know.

Why did Australia go to Vietnam, and who really asked?
Circle one: South Vietnam asked, and Australia answered · Australia asked to be asked · Both
are partly true · We can’t know, from these records, who first raised the idea · Another finding,
written below


  MY FINDING
  My finding. ________________________________________________
  ______________________________________________________________
  The one piece of evidence that most changed my mind. ________
  ______________________________________________________________
  What I still can’t know. ___________________________________
  ______________________________________________________________




Why it still matters
The war divided families, streets and Parliament. Veterans, national servicemen, conscientious
objectors, marchers, and Vietnamese families who came to Australia after 1975 remember it in
different ways. Asking who asked is also asking who decides when a country goes to war, and
who has a say. Many of the men in the ballot were too young to vote.

Open these investigations in the app: robmac10.github.io/vietnam-case/#sleuth


  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  1. The “lottery of death”
  In 1917, during the second conscription referendum campaign, Henry Boote of the Australian Worker
  was prosecuted and fined £100 for articles that included “The Lottery of Death” (Australian
  Dictionary of Biography). In the 1960s Arthur Calwell revived the phrase for the birthday ballot
  (Shrine of Remembrance; Museum of Australian Democracy). The Australian War Memorial says
  simply that opponents called it that. This file has not found the phrase in Calwell’s own recorded
  words.
  Question. Why does it matter who first used a phrase, and how could you check?




  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  2. Who asked whom?
  The National Museum of Australia says the Australian Ambassador in Saigon was instructed to press
  Quat, and that Quat gave verbal agreement about three hours before Menzies spoke. Historians such
  as Michael Sexton and the official historian Peter Edwards describe a request arranged after Australia
  had offered troops. In 1971 McMahon pointed out that earlier South Vietnamese leaders had made
  general appeals for help, in July and December 1964.
  Question. If a request is arranged after an offer, is it still a request? What would you need to see to
  decide?




  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  3. Counting the dead at Long Tan
  The Australian count, used by the Australian War Memorial and the official history, is 245 enemy
  bodies found, with three soldiers captured. Vietnamese accounts put their dead at around 150. A
  2016 study by a retired Australian brigadier and Vietnamese linguist listed 176 named dead from one
  regiment. Higher figures, from 500 to more than 1,600, rest on documents that have never been
  produced or corroborated, or on claims that researchers have called false.

Question. Why might each side count differently, and what would make a count reliable?




STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
4. How many marched, and how many were arrested?
Melbourne, 8 May 1970: about 70,000 (National Museum of Australia) or about 100,000 (estimates
by many who were there, cited by the historian Ken Mansell). Sydney, 18 September 1970: 173
arrested (National Museum of Australia; Australian War Memorial) or more than 200 (Mansell).
Adelaide, the same day: about 130 (State Library of South Australia) or 141 (Mansell).
Question. Who counts a crowd, and why might police, organisers and newspapers get different
numbers?




STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
5. FOLKLORE, not history: what happened to Harold Holt?
No evidence supports these stories. A Chinese submarine: from a former naval officer via Anthony
Grey’s book The Prime Minister Was a Spy (1983); Holt’s biographer Tom Frame called it a
fabrication (2005). The CIA: no source or evidence has been traced. Suicide: rumour only; the 1968
police report found his mood normal. The coroner (2005) called the theories “fanciful”.
Question. Why do stories grow when there is no body and no inquiry?




STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
6. How many national servicemen went to Vietnam?
The Australian War Memorial gives 15,381. The Department of Veterans’ Affairs’ Anzac Portal says
some 18,000. The National Archives says over 19,000. Aboriginal men could volunteer, but did not
have to register for the ballot (Anzac Portal).
Question. Three official sources give three totals. What might each one be counting?

pages.text:
VIETNAM AND THE BIRTHDAY BALLOT, 1964–1972 · YEAR 10 · TEACHER

Teacher Note
NOTE


This note is for the teacher. It is not a student page.


What’s true about the opener
This note is not part of the student page. Steve, his family and the notebook are constructed for
this file, and the opener carries an Imagined badge. Steve is not based on any real soldier. He is
given no unit, no battle, no date and no cause of death, so that he cannot be mistaken for one of
the Australians who died. Please do not ask students to find “the real Steve.” What is true
behind the page: the ballot drew birth dates from a barrel; 20-year-old men could be called up;
the federal voting age was 21; and the battalion was announced on 29 April 1965, the same date
as the exchange of letters.


Care this case needs
Some students will have family who served, were called up, refused, marched or came to
Australia from Vietnam after 1975. The language of Anzac was later applied to Vietnam service:
a Department of Veterans’ Affairs resource, Vietnam: Our War – Our Peace, calls those who
served “torch-bearers of the Anzac tradition forged with the landing at Gallipoli on 25 April
1915” (see the Anzac case). Living people, including veterans and protest figures, are not named
on the student pages unless they are quoted from a public record; no living veteran is quoted.
Long Tan is given at the level of outcome, without graphic detail. A Minister’s often-quoted
1970 insult of the Moratorium marchers (National Museum of Australia) is not reproduced,
because it uses the language of sexual violence. Do not ask students to role-play the dead, or to
invent words for anyone named in this file.


Source conflicts, flagged
Several figures differ between reliable sources, and the student pages give ranges with their
sources rather than a single number. National servicemen in Vietnam: 15,381 (AWM), some
18,000 (Anzac Portal), over 19,000 (NAA). Total called up: 63,740 (AWM) or some 63,000
(NAA). Australian deaths in the war: 524 (Australian War Memorial and Department of
Veterans’ Affairs, 2026); earlier Memorial pages give 523. Australians who served: more than
60,000 (AWM) or almost 60,000 (Anzac Portal). Holt’s “all the way with LBJ”: 29 June 1966
(PM Transcripts 1339; the American Presidency Project); the National Archives says July 1966,
and some writers give 30 June. The Holt theories in Super Sleuths are folklore: teach them as
examples of how rumour grows, not as possibilities. Moratorium crowds and arrests: see Super
Sleuths. Long Tan, Australian dead: 17 killed in action and one died of wounds, so 18 in all
(AWM; McNeill, To Long Tan, 1993). Long Tan, Vietnamese dead: 245 bodies counted (AWM;
McNeill); around 150 (Vietnamese accounts, reported in The Conversation, 2016); 176 named
from the 275th Regiment (E. Chamberlain, 2016, reported in the Sydney Morning Herald);

pages.text:
figures of 500, 800, 878 and 1,632 are uncorroborated or shown to be false. The phrase “lottery
of death” goes back to 1917, when Henry Boote, editor of the Australian Worker, was fined £100
for articles that included “The Lottery of Death” (Australian Dictionary of Biography). The
Shrine of Remembrance and the Museum of Australian Democracy say Arthur Calwell revived
it in the 1960s; his own recorded words using it have not been found for this file. The date of the
first ballot, 10 March 1965, and the total of sixteen ballots to 22 September 1972, are given by
the Department of Veterans’ Affairs’ Anzac Portal; they have not been checked against NAA
series MP1357/63.


The request, and what is still argued
Menzies told the House there was “a request.” The letters show an Australian offer, confirmed
in writing, and a South Vietnamese acceptance and request, on the same day. The National
Museum of Australia says Menzies “somewhat misled parliament” by implying the request
came first. Some classroom sources go further and say there was no request at all. This file does
not settle that. Edwards (the official history, Crises and Commitments, 1992) and Sexton (War
for the Asking, 1981; 2002) agree that Australia took the initiative; they differ in tone. Remind
students that SEATO itself was never formally invoked for Vietnam (Vietnam Generation, vol.
3, no. 2, 1991).


A local memory, kept apart from the record
The author’s recollection is of ending up at Brisbane City Hall and King George Square, with
William (Billy) and Sonia McMahon there. It is a personal memory, offered for teachers, not a
verified report, and it is not on the student pages. The dates suggest it belongs to 1971, not to
the 1970 Moratoriums. John Gorton was Prime Minister from 10 January 1968 to 10 March
1971, so he was Prime Minister for both 1970 Moratoriums (National Archives of Australia).
McMahon became Prime Minister on 10 March 1971. A media release datelined Brisbane, 8
April 1971, records his meeting in the Premier’s Office with Joh Bjelke-Petersen; it says he came
to Queensland at the Premier’s invitation (PM Transcripts 2402). His speech notes for the
Queensland Liberal Convention on Sunday 13 June 1971 begin: “This is my second visit to
Queensland since I became Prime Minister” (PM Transcripts 2430). Neither document
mentions City Hall, King George Square, Sonia McMahon or any protest, and the June notes do
not name the venue. Later visits, in 1971 or 1972, have not been checked. The third Moratorium
(30 June 1971) came after both visits. Teachers can use this as a model of checking a memory
against the record: the memory is not wrong for being unrecorded, and the record is not
complete for leaving it out.


Curriculum
Australian Curriculum v9, Year 10 History, The globalising world (an optional sub-strand):
AC9HH10K16 (the fear of communism and the Cold War in Australian society), AC9HH10K18
(an elaboration names conscription and the Vietnam War), and AC9HH10K20 (historical

Placement
In this chronological book the case is placed by Menzies’ announcement of 29 April 1965. It
follows the Freedom Ride (February 1965) and comes before Mabo (1992). The file covers 1964,
when the ballot was legislated, to December 1972, when the call-up stopped.


Pictures
Robert Menzies and Arthur Calwell are shown as plain silhouettes with name cards, not
likenesses. The Quat letter is a document silhouette, not a facsimile. No photographs of
soldiers, of the dead, or of protesters are used. This case does not use First Nations material.


Sources
Primary. Commonwealth Parliamentary Debates, House of Representatives: 29 April 1965
(Menzies), vol. 45, pp. 1060–1; 4 May 1965 (Calwell), vol. 46, pp. 1102–7 (page references as
cited by the ANZAC Day Commemoration Committee; check against ParlInfo). PM Transcripts:
1105 (Menzies, 29 April 1965); 2459 (Vietnam correspondence, 19 August 1971); 2402
(Brisbane, 8 April 1971); 2430 (Queensland Liberal Convention, 13 June 1971). Southeast Asia
Collective Defense Treaty (Manila, 8 September 1954), art. IV(3). NAA series MP1357/63, the
ballot barrel and marbles. Harold Holt. PM Transcripts 1339 (remarks at the White House, 29
June 1966). National Archives of Australia, “Harold Holt: during office” (Australia’s Prime
Ministers) and “Harold Holt’s disappearance” (fact sheet; police report on file A1209,
1968/8063). Victorian State Coroner, finding of 2 September 2005, as reported by ABC News,
The Age and the Sydney Morning Herald (2 September 2005). The Age, “Source behind Holt-
to-China theory discredited” (5 August 2005), on Tom Frame, The Life and Death of Harold
Holt (2005). National Film and Sound Archive, “Allegations and conspiracy theories” (from The
Harold Holt Mystery, Ten Network, 1985). Reference. National Archives of Australia, “National
service, 1965–72” (fact sheet); “John Gorton” (Australia’s Prime Ministers). Australian War
Memorial: “Vietnam War 1962–75”; “Long Tan”; Ashley Ekins, “A very close thing indeed,”
Wartime 55; “What is a Nasho or National Serviceman?”; poster C96416. Department of
Veterans’ Affairs, Anzac Portal, “Conscription and the birthday ballot during the Vietnam War.”
National Museum of Australia, Defining Moments: “Vietnam moratoriums” and “Australian
troops committed to Vietnam.” Museum of Australian Democracy, “The National Service Act
1964.” State Library of South Australia, Campaign for Peace in Vietnam sticker. Ken Mansell,
“The Gloves Come Off,” Labour History Melbourne, 2020. Peter Edwards with Gregory
Pemberton, Crises and Commitments (1992); Peter Edwards, “Australian Government and the
Involvement in the Vietnam War,” Vietnam Generation 3:2 (1991). Michael Sexton, War for the
Asking (1981; 2002). Ian McNeill, To Long Tan (1993). Lindsay Murdoch, Sydney Morning
Herald, 21 April 2016. The Conversation, “The battle over Long Tan’s memory – a perspective
from Viet Nam,” 2016.

A NOTE BEFORE YOU READ
  This case names Torres Strait Islander people who have died, including Eddie Koiki Mabo (died 21
  January 1992). This investigation acknowledges the Meriam people of Mer, and follows AIATSIS
  guidance. No photograph of Eddie Koiki Mabo is used. A note for teachers is at the end of the case.




MABO AND TERRA NULLIUS, 1982–1992 · YEAR 10 · READ
Mabo and terra nullius, 1982–1992
Was Australia ever really treated as ‘nobody’s land’?


What is agreed
Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber, used in Super Sleuths, marks what is still disputed or was
added later.


  Eddie Koiki Mabo was a Meriam man from Mer (Murray Island) in the Torres Strait. In May
  1982 he and other Meriam plaintiffs, including David Passi, Sam Passi, Celuia Mapo Salee and
  James Rice, began a case in the High Court about ownership of land on the Murray Islands.




  While the case was running, the Queensland Parliament passed the Queensland Coast Islands
  Declaratory Act 1985. Section 3 declared that, on annexation, the islands “were vested in the
  Crown in right of Queensland freed from all other rights, interests and claims of any kind
  whatsoever.” Section 5 said no compensation “was or is payable.”




  In Mabo v Queensland (No 1), decided 8 December 1988, the High Court held that the 1985 Act
  was invalid to the extent it was inconsistent with the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth). The
  land case could go on.




  Eddie Mabo died on 21 January 1992. On 3 June 1992, in Mabo v Queensland (No 2), six of the
  seven High Court justices held that the common law of Australia can recognise native title, and
  that the Meriam people were entitled, as against the whole world, to the possession, use,
  occupation and enjoyment of most of the lands of the Murray Islands (subject to some particular
  Crown interests).




  Justice Brennan’s leading reasons discussed and rejected what he called an “enlarged notion of

Each witness is a real person, or a real set of words from the record. A period portrait is used

Ask the same three questions of each.

                                  Eddie Koiki Mabo
                                  Meriam man of Mer (Murray Island) · lead plaintiff · died 21 January 1992,
                                  before the High Court decided the land case

                                  Interviewed on his land at Las, Mer, in 1989, and remembered in later
                                  museum and film records.
                                  What they said
                                  The National Museum quotes him: “My father told me: ‘Son, this land will
                                  belong to you when I die.’” In 1989, on the land at Las, he said: “There were
 A silhouette, not a likeness.
                                  a total of 18 generations before my grandfather’s time that occupied this
      No public-domain
  photograph of Eddie Koiki       land and of course, from my grandfather to my father and myself makes it
 Mabo is used, out of respect;    up to 20 generations all together. That we’ve occupied this area.” He
 a silhouette is used instead.    described how later, after the London Missionary Society came, people
                                  were moved to the front village.
                                  Could they have seen it?
                                  He was speaking about his own family’s land and Meriam memory, not
                                  about a Latin phrase in a law book. He was a plaintiff, not a judge. He did
                                  not live to hear the judgment of 3 June 1992.
                                  Why might they say it?
                                  To say, on the record, that the land at Las had been held through
                                  generations, and that it would belong to him when his father died. This file
                                  keeps his recorded words, and does not invent what he would have said on

pages.text:
Justice Brennan
                                  Justice of the High Court of Australia · leading reasons in Mabo (No 2), 3 June
                                  1992

                                  A written judgment, not a speech from the street.
                                  What they said
                                  Brennan J wrote that “the fiction by which the rights and interests of
                                  indigenous inhabitants in land were treated as non-existent was justified by
                                  a policy which has no place in the contemporary law of this country.” He
A silhouette, not a likeness.
                                  also wrote: “It is imperative in today’s world that the common law should
 Official judicial portraits
   remain in copyright.           neither be nor be seen to be frozen in an age of racial discrimination.” He
                                  said the common law “would perpetuate injustice if it were to continue to
                                  embrace the enlarged notion of terra nullius and persist in characterizing
                                  the indigenous inhabitants of the Australian colonies as people too low in
                                  the scale of social organization to be acknowledged as possessing rights and
                                  interests in land.”
                                  Could they have seen it?
                                  He was deciding a case in 1992, from evidence and earlier law, including
                                  findings made in the Queensland Supreme Court. He was not an eyewitness
                                  to 1788, or to life on Mer. A judgment is an official interpretation of the law,
                                  written for a reason, by a judge in the majority.
                                  Why might they say it?
                                  To explain why the Court would no longer treat Indigenous people as if they
                                  had no rights in land, and to give reasons for recognising native title in
                                  Australian common law.
                                  Source. Mabo v Queensland (No 2) [1992] HCA 23; (1992) 175 CLR 1, Brennan J. The
                                  judgment is on AustLII.

The State of Queensland
                                 Defendant in the Mabo litigation · Parliament of Queensland, 1985

                                 The government’s case, in the words of a statute passed while the Meriam
                                 claim was already before the courts.
                                 What they said
                                 The long title was “An Act to allay any doubts that may exist concerning
                                 certain islands forming part of Queensland.” Section 3 declared that, on
                                 annexation, “the islands were vested in the Crown in right of Queensland
   A document mark, not a
 likeness. The witness is the
                                 freed from all other rights, interests and claims of any kind whatsoever and
     State of Queensland,        became waste lands of the Crown.” Section 5 declared: “No compensation
speaking through a 1985 Act      was or is payable to any person” by reason of the annexation, or in respect
        of Parliament.
                                 of any right, interest or claim alleged to have existed before it, or by reason
                                 of any later disposal.
                                 Could they have seen it?
                                 This is not one person’s memory. It is a Parliament changing, or trying to
                                 declare, the legal consequences of annexation in 1879. The High Court in
                                 1988 treated the declarations as an attempt to extinguish the very rights the
                                 Meriam plaintiffs were claiming. A statute can be evidence of a
                                 government’s position. It is not evidence of how the islands were actually
                                 occupied.
                                 Why might they say it?
                                 The Act’s own title said it was to “allay any doubts.” Passed while the
                                 Meriam case was already before the courts, it tried to declare the islands
                                 free of other rights, with no compensation. Students can ask what that
                                 timing shows.

My finding
MABO AND TERRA NULLIUS, 1982–1992 · YEAR 10 · DECIDE

The three witness cards are Eddie Koiki Mabo, Justice Brennan, and the State of Queensland, speaking through the
1985 Act.

There is no answer at the back. The narrator of the notebook is invented. The quoted words, the
1985 Act, and the dates are not. Eddie Mabo did not hear the judgment. Write only what these
records can support. One of the findings you may choose is that we can’t know.

Was Australia ever really treated as ‘nobody’s land’?
Circle one: The law did treat Indigenous land rights as if they were not there · The Latin phrase
terra nullius is a later label, and the earlier official language used other words · The 1985 Act shows
Queensland trying to declare the islands nobody else’s, after the case had begun · We can’t know,
from this file, exactly when the Latin phrase entered Australian legal usage · Another finding, written
below

Why it still matters
The 1992 judgment is still taught as a turning point, and the phrase terra nullius is still argued
over. Families on Mer, and native-title law after 1993, did not end on 3 June 1992. A careful
finding will say what the records show, and what they cannot say for people who were not
asked, or who did not live to hear the result.

  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  1. The phrase debate
  Brennan J describes a “fiction” that treated Indigenous land rights as non-existent, and an “enlarged
  notion of terra nullius.” Historians and some lawyers, including David Ritter, have asked when the
  Latin phrase itself was first used in Australian law, and whether earlier official language used other
  words for a similar idea.
  Question. What changes when a later Latin label is treated as if it had been the official slogan of
  1788?




  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  2. The 1985 Act, and Mabo (No 1)
  The Queensland Coast Islands Declaratory Act was assented to on 15 April 1985, while the Meriam
  case was already before the courts. In 1988 the High Court held it invalid to the extent it clashed with
  the Racial Discrimination Act 1975.
  Question. Why might a government pass a declaratory Act after a land case has already begun, and
  what did the 1988 decision change?




  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  3. He never heard the judgment
  Eddie Koiki Mabo died on 21 January 1992. The High Court decided Mabo (No 2) on 3 June 1992.
  This file does not invent what he would have said that day.
  Question. What does a gap like that ask you to do, and what does it ask you not to do?

pages.text:
STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
4. What the 1992 orders did, and did not do
The Court recognised native title, and Meriam rights in most of the Murray Islands, subject to some
particular Crown interests. The Native Title Act 1993 followed. This file does not pretend the decision
“gave the land back” in a simple way to all First Nations people, and it does not try the later cases.
Question. What can one judgment settle, and what does it leave open?




STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
5. Fact-finding on Mer
Fact-finding by Moynihan J in the Queensland Supreme Court did not accept all of Eddie Mabo’s
particular claims to individual land. The High Court still recognised Meriam native title in most of
the islands. Both of those things can be true at once.
Question. Why might a court accept a people’s title, and still not accept every individual claim made
in the evidence?

IMAGINED Written for this case, based on real events, not a real document.
                                                               A science room, last period
                      A constructed notebook · not a historical document
Miss put a jar of sand on the bench and turned the lights off.
She said that is how the scientists treated it. Sand from deep in
the ground at Madjedbebe, a rock shelter on Mirarr Country in
Arnhem Land, was taken out and kept in the dark, because
sunlight resets the clock.
A grain of quartz slowly stores up energy while it is buried. In
a laboratory it can be made to give that energy back as a tiny
flash of light. More light, longer underground. So the date is
not written on anything. It is counted, grain by grain.
The team who dug there say people were living at Madjedbebe
around 65,000 years ago. Another team says the numbers do not
fit, and that termites and rain can move things down through
sand. The Mirarr people agreed to the dig, and they had the right
to stop it.

  I wrote 65,000 in my book. Then I put a question mark
                        next to it.

pages.text:
A NOTE BEFORE YOU READ
  Madjedbebe is on Mirarr Country, in Arnhem Land. This investigation acknowledges the Mirarr
  people, the Traditional Owners of the site, and uses only published, cited public records. It shows no
  images of the rock shelter or its art, and retells no cultural stories. If something here should be
  corrected, please tell the teacher who shared this investigation. A note for teachers is at the end of the
  case.




MADJEDBEBE · YEAR 7 · READ
Madjedbebe: dating the sand
How old is Madjedbebe, and how sure can anyone be?


What is agreed
Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber, used in Super Sleuths, marks what is still disputed or was
added later.


  Madjedbebe is a rock shelter on the western edge of the Arnhem Land plateau in the Northern
  Territory, on Mirarr Country. It was formerly known as Malakunanja II. It sits on Aboriginal
  land inside the Jabiluka mining lease, which is surrounded by Kakadu National Park.




  The site was excavated in 1973 and in 1989. Sediments from the 1989 dig were dated to about
  60,000 to 50,000 years ago, using thermoluminescence and optically stimulated luminescence
  (OSL) dating. Those ages were argued over, mainly because of doubts about whether the
  artefacts had stayed in the layers where they were found.




  A team led by archaeologist Chris Clarkson of the University of Queensland dug at Madjedbebe
  again in 2012 and 2015. The dating was led by Zenobia Jacobs of the University of Wollongong.
  The work was done under an agreement with the Gundjeihmi Aboriginal Corporation, which
  represents the Mirarr. Under it, the Mirarr had a right to stop the dig at any time, control over
  the artefacts, and a final say on the findings announced.




  The team’s results were published in the journal Nature on 20 July 2017. The paper said that
  human occupation began around 65,000 years ago. The lowest dense band of artefacts was
  given a modelled start of about 65,000 years ago and an end of about 52,700 years ago, each
  with a margin of error of several thousand years.




                            Reopen the Record: Australian Histories · sample ·   228

pages.alt: Page 229. Madjedbebe. OSL dating does not date a stone tool. It measures how long ago grains of sand were last in sunlight. A date for a tool depends on the tool staying in the same layer as the sand around it. In 2018
pages.text:
OSL dating does not date a stone tool. It measures how long ago grains of sand were last in
sunlight. A date for a tool depends on the tool staying in the same layer as the sand around it.




In 2018 archaeologists James O’Connell, Jim Allen and colleagues published a paper in PNAS
(Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences). They called the ages anomalous, and argued
that artefacts could have moved down through the sand. The argument has continued in later
papers. This file records both sides. It does not settle the question.




                       Reopen the Record: Australian Histories · sample ·   229

Three witnesses
MADJEDBEBE · YEAR 7 · ASK


Each witness is a real person, or a real set of words from the record. A period portrait is used
where one exists and is free to reuse. Otherwise you will see a plain silhouette, not a likeness.
Ask the same three questions of each.

                                   Chris Clarkson, Zenobia Jacobs and colleagues
                                   Archaeologists and a dating specialist · Excavated Madjedbebe in 2012 and 2015
                                   · Nature, 20 July 2017

                                   The team who dug the site, dated the sand and published the 65,000-year
                                   result.
                                   What they said
                                   “Human occupation began around 65,000 years ago, with a distinctive
                                   stone tool assemblage including grinding stones, ground ochres, reflective
 A document silhouette, not a
                                   additives and ground-edge hatchet heads.” They wrote that this “sets a new
 facsimile. Nature, July 2017.     minimum age for human arrival in Australia,” and that “the total age
                                   uncertainties are only 3–4 kyr” (thousand years) for the sand samples
                                   linked to the lowest dense band of artefacts.
                                   Could they have seen it?
                                   They were there, layer by layer, and they measured the sand themselves.
                                   They are the best-placed witnesses to what was in the ground. But a
                                   luminescence date is a date for when sand was last in sunlight. Linking that
                                   date to a stone tool depends on the tool not having moved. Their paper
                                   argues that it had not moved, using pieces of stone that fit back together
                                   and other tests.
                                   Why might they say it?
                                   To report a major result, carefully, in a journal that checks papers before
                                   they are published. Scientists also argue for their own methods, and a very
                                   old date is big news. Students can ask both questions: how good is the
                                   evidence, and who has a stake in the answer?
                                   Source. C. Clarkson, Z. Jacobs, B. Marwick and others, “Human occupation of northern
                                   Australia by 65,000 years ago,” Nature 547 (2017), pp. 306–310. Quoted from the published
                                   abstract and main text. The image is a document silhouette, not a facsimile.

                                   What did they say they saw? · Could they really have seen it? · Why might they say it?

pages.alt: Page 231. Madjedbebe. James O’Connell, Jim Allen and colleagues Archaeologists · Did not dig at Madjedbebe in 2012 or 2015 · PNAS, August 2018 Critics who read the published data and argued that the 65,000-year date does
pages.text:
James O’Connell, Jim Allen and colleagues
                                Archaeologists · Did not dig at Madjedbebe in 2012 or 2015 · PNAS, August 2018

                                Critics who read the published data and argued that the 65,000-year date
                                does not fit the wider evidence.
                                What they said
                                “In the context of Sahul and the wider region, these ages are anomalous.”
                                They wrote that “these mismatches demand critical review,” and that sandy
                                deposits in the tropics are open to many kinds of disturbance, “most
A document silhouette, not a    notably, bioturbation by termites.” They also pointed to a radiocarbon date
   facsimile. PNAS, 2018.       of about 13,000 years on charcoal from the same depth in the 1989 dig,
                                which the excavators had called intrusive.
                                Could they have seen it?
                                They did not dig in 2012 or 2015. They worked from the published reports
                                and from comparisons with many other sites across the region. That is a
                                real kind of evidence: if one site is far older than all the others, it is fair to
                                ask why. But a comparison with other sites cannot prove what happened
                                inside this one.
                                Why might they say it?
                                To test a big claim, which is how science is meant to work. They also had
                                their own view that people reached Sahul (Australia and New Guinea joined
                                at low sea levels) closer to 50,000 years ago. Students can ask whether a
                                critic who already holds a different date is more careful, or less open, or
                                both.
                                Source. J. F. O’Connell, J. Allen and others, “When did Homo sapiens first reach Southeast
                                Asia and Sahul?”, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 115, no. 34 (2018), pp.
                                8482–8490. Quoted from the section on Madjedbebe. The image is a document silhouette,
                                not a facsimile.

Gundjeihmi Aboriginal Corporation
                                   Represents the Mirarr Traditional Owners · Partner in the 2012 and 2015
                                   excavations · Media release, 19 July 2017

                                   The organisation of the people whose Country the site is on, and who
                                   controlled the terms of the dig.
                                   What they said
                                   “A team of archaeologists and dating specialists have new proof that
                                   Aboriginal people have been in Australia for at least 65,000 years — much
 A document silhouette, not a
                                   longer than the 47,000 years believed by some archaeologists.” The release
facsimile. Media release, July     described the agreement as “giving access to country for the research team
            2017.                  and providing the Mirarr with unprecedented control over the operations of
                                   the excavation and its findings.” Its chief executive, Justin O’Brien, said:
                                   “These findings reinforce the need for the highest level of conservation and
                                   protection for this site.”
                                   Could they have seen it?
                                   The Corporation did not do the dating. Its release reports the scientists’
                                   result. It could speak with authority about the agreement, about who
                                   controlled the dig, and about the place itself.
                                   Why might they say it?
                                   To share important news about Mirarr Country, to show a model of
                                   research done in partnership, and to argue for protecting the site, which
                                   lies inside a uranium mining lease. Students can ask how a result reads
                                   differently when it comes from the Traditional Owners rather than from a
                                   journal.
                                   Source. Gundjeihmi Aboriginal Corporation, “Kakadu site of Australia’s earliest home,”
                                   media release, 19 July 2017, mirarr.net. Quoted from the published release. No photograph

My finding
MADJEDBEBE · YEAR 7 · DECIDE

The three witness cards are the excavation team, their critics, and the Gundjeihmi Aboriginal Corporation. Further
questions — the charcoal, the deeper artefacts and the agreement — are in Super Sleuths.

You have a constructed notebook, a short agreed file, and three witnesses. The opening page is
not a historical document. Say how old you think the evidence at Madjedbebe is, and how sure
you can be. “We can’t know” is an honest finding when careful scientists disagree. Do not invent
a number the sources do not give.

How old is Madjedbebe, and how sure can anyone be?
Circle one: About 65,000 years: the dating is sound · Younger, closer to 50,000 years: things moved
in the sand · Older than 65,000 years: the deepest artefacts count · We can’t know an exact age,
but people were there for tens of thousands of years · We can’t know, from this file · Another
finding, written below


  MY FINDING
  My finding. ________________________________________________
  ______________________________________________________________
  The one piece of evidence that most changed my mind. ________
  ______________________________________________________________
  What I still can’t know. ___________________________________
  ______________________________________________________________




Why it still matters
A number like 65,000 travels fast. It appears in speeches, in classrooms and on signs. The file is
open because the number came from sand, not from a label, and because scientists are still
testing it. Who controls a dig, who announces the result, and who gets to say how old a place is,
are questions about the present as well as the past.

MADJEDBEBE · YEAR 7 · SUPER SLEUTHS
Super Sleuths
Go further only if you want to. Amber marks what is still disputed, or what later writers added.
Madjedbebe is on Mirarr Country. This file uses published public records only, and shows no images of
the site or its art.
Open these investigations in the app: robmac10.github.io/madjedbebe-case/#sleuth


 STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
 1. The notebook is written for this file
 The typed page is a constructed student voice in a science room. The narrator is not a historical
 person. The opener does not quote any scientist or Traditional Owner. The facts in it (the dark, the
 grains, 65,000, the right to stop the dig) are from the agreed file.
 Question. Which sentences in the notebook can you check against the agreed file, and which are only
 the narrator’s feelings?




 2. What does a luminescence date measure?
 Optically stimulated luminescence measures the energy stored in quartz grains since they were last in
 sunlight. Samples are collected so that light cannot reach them. The date belongs to the sand. It
 becomes a date for a stone tool only if the tool and the sand have stayed together.
 Question. What would have to be true for the date of the sand to also be the date of the tool?




 STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
 3. The charcoal that did not fit
 A piece of charcoal from about the same depth in the 1989 dig gave a radiocarbon date of about
 12,800–13,000 years. The excavators said it had probably fallen or blown in during the dig. Their
 critics said that answer was not explained. Radiocarbon dating cannot reach back much beyond
 about 50,000 years, so it cannot test a 65,000-year date directly.
 Question. If one date disagrees with eighteen others, when is it fair to set it aside, and when should it
 make you doubt the rest?




 STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER

                          Reopen the Record: Australian Histories · sample ·   234

pages.alt: Page 235. Madjedbebe. 4. Deeper still? Below the dense band, the published data list hundreds of artefacts in sand dated to about 65,000 to 87,000 years. The excavators thought most had settled down from above. Some
pages.text:
4. Deeper still?
Below the dense band, the published data list hundreds of artefacts in sand dated to about 65,000 to
87,000 years. The excavators thought most had settled down from above. Some newspapers in July
2017 reported occupation “up to 80,000 years ago.” The Nature paper itself argued for about 65,000.
Question. Why might a newspaper headline choose a bigger number than the scientists’ own paper?




STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
5. Who controls a dig?
Under the 2012–2015 agreement, the Mirarr could stop the dig, controlled the artefacts, and had a
final say on what was announced. Reports at the time said the artefacts were to be returned to the
Mirarr. The site is inside the Jabiluka uranium mining lease.
Question. How might an agreement like this change what a team is allowed to find, keep and say? Is
that a weakness, a strength, or both?




6. Sure, maybe, or a guess?
Sure: Madjedbebe is on Mirarr Country; it was dug in 1973, 1989, 2012 and 2015; the 2017 Nature
paper dated first occupation to around 65,000 years ago using OSL; other archaeologists dispute that
age. Maybe: whether the artefacts stayed in place; whether people arrived earlier still. A guess: an
exact year, or what anyone at Madjedbebe was thinking. The opener is not a source.
Question. Write a finding of no more than five sentences, and mark each sentence sure, maybe, or a
guess.

Teacher Note
MADJEDBEBE · YEAR 7 · TEACHER NOTE


This note is for the teacher. It is not a student page.


What’s true about the opener
The typographic page is a constructed student notebook, written for this file and marked
Imagined. It is not a historical document and it quotes no one. Its science (quartz grains,
sunlight, stored energy released as light) is a plain description of optically stimulated
luminescence. The site facts in it come from the agreed file.


Curriculum
Year 7 History, Deep time history of Australia. Lead code AC9HH7K02 (theories about the
causes and effects of the arrival of early First Nations Australians on the continent). Also
AC9HH7K08 (methods and sources used by historians and archaeologists, and the importance
of conserving heritage) and AC9HH7K03 (First Nations Australians as the world’s oldest
continuing cultures). Codes checked against the v9 Year 7 History content descriptions.


Country, and care
Madjedbebe is on Mirarr Country. The shelter is known for its rock art, and no image of the art
or the shelter is used. No cultural stories are retold. The only voice of the Traditional Owners
used is the public media release of the Gundjeihmi Aboriginal Corporation. Living Mirarr
Traditional Owners were quoted in the press in 2017; those quotes are not reproduced here.
Teachers wishing to add community voices should follow the protocols of the Gundjeihmi
Aboriginal Corporation and the AIATSIS Code of Ethics.


Source conflicts, flagged
Nature’s online abstract and the published article word the toolkit slightly differently
(“grindstones … groundedge axes” and “grinding stones … ground-edge hatchet heads”); this
file quotes the published version. The dispute over Madjedbebe is live: O’Connell, Allen and
colleagues (2018) and Williams and colleagues (Geoarchaeology, 2021) argue for disturbance;
the excavators and others have replied. Students should not be told the matter is settled either
way. “47,000 years” in the Corporation’s release refers to the younger estimates favoured by
some archaeologists at the time.


Pictures
All three witness images are document silhouettes, labelled as such. No photographs of people,
of the site, or of its art are used. The QR emblem is a drawn pattern of sand layers and one
bright grain, not a cultural design.

pages.text:
IMAGINED Written for this case, based on real events, not a real document.
                                                                   History. The whiteboard.
                      A constructed notebook · not a historical document
Sir wrote three numbers on the board and crossed out two of
them.
About 26,000. Then 62,000. Then 40,000. All for the same place, a
dry lake in south-western New South Wales, on the Country of
the Barkindji, Ngiyampaa and Mutthi Mutthi peoples.
He said nobody lied. They used different clocks. One counts
carbon. One counts uranium and the damage it does to teeth. One
counts light trapped in sand.
I asked which clock is right. He said that is the case.

    I copied all three numbers. I didn’t cross any out.

A NOTE BEFORE YOU READ
  Lake Mungo is in the Willandra Lakes Region, the Country of the Barkindji (Paakantji), Ngiyampaa
  and Mutthi Mutthi peoples. This investigation acknowledges them as Traditional Owners and uses
  only published, cited public records. It refers to ancestral remains only as public records do. It shows
  no images of remains and does not describe burials. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are
  advised that it refers to people who have died. If something here should be corrected, please tell the
  teacher who shared this investigation. A note for teachers is at the end of the case.




LAKE MUNGO · YEAR 7 · READ
Lake Mungo: how do scientists date the past?
How old is the oldest evidence at Lake Mungo, and why did the answer keep
changing?


What is agreed
Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber, used in Super Sleuths, marks what is still disputed or was
added later.


  Lake Mungo is one of the Willandra Lakes in south-western New South Wales. The lakes have
  been dry for thousands of years. Along the eastern shore of Lake Mungo is a long crescent-
  shaped dune, called a lunette, whose layers of sand and clay record changes in the lake. The
  Willandra Lakes Region was placed on the World Heritage List in 1981.




  The region is the Country of the Barkindji (Paakantji), Ngiyampaa and Mutthi Mutthi peoples,
  who continue to have close connections to the Willandra Lakes.




  In 1968 geologist Jim Bowler found human remains eroding from the lunette. They are known
  publicly as Mungo Lady. In 1974 he found the remains of a man, known publicly as Mungo Man.
  Scientists have also used the names Mungo I and Mungo III.




  Different methods have given different ages. Early radiocarbon estimates placed Mungo Lady at
  about 20,000 to 26,000 years ago. Estimates for Mungo Man have included about 30,000 years,
  42,000–45,000 years, and, in 1999, 62,000 years.




                            Reopen the Record: Australian Histories · sample ·   241

pages.alt: Page 242. Lake Mungo. In 2003 a team led by Jim Bowler published 25 new optical (OSL) ages in the journal Nature. They concluded that both people lived about 40,000 years ago (give or take 2,000 years), and that people
pages.text:
In 2003 a team led by Jim Bowler published 25 new optical (OSL) ages in the journal Nature.
They concluded that both people lived about 40,000 years ago (give or take 2,000 years), and
that people were at Lake Mungo by 50,000 to 46,000 years ago.




Mungo Lady was returned to Lake Mungo in 1992. Mungo Man was returned to Country in
November 2017, with 103 other ancestral remains. In 2022 the Australian Government
approved a proposal to rebury the ancestral remains on Country. Traditional Owners have not
all agreed about how the ancestors should rest. This file does not take a side.




                      Reopen the Record: Australian Histories · sample ·   242
