Three witnesses
LAKE MUNGO · YEAR 7 · ASK


Each witness is a real person, or a real set of words from the record. A period portrait is used
where one exists and is free to reuse. Otherwise you will see a plain silhouette, not a likeness.
Ask the same three questions of each.

                                  Alan Thorne and colleagues
                                  Anthropologist and dating scientists · Australian National University and others
                                  · Journal of Human Evolution, June 1999 · Thorne died in 2012

                                  The team who dated Mungo Man directly, using uranium in the bones and
                                  teeth, and reached the oldest date of all.
                                  What they said
                                  “The best age estimate for the human skeleton is obtained through the
                                  combination of U-series and ESR analyses yielding 62,000 ± 6000 years.”
 A document silhouette, not a
                                  They wrote that this was “in close agreement with OSL age estimates on the
 facsimile. Journal of Human      sediment … of 61,000 ± 2000 years,” and that all their results “are
       Evolution, 1999.           considerably older than the previously assumed age of LM3 and
                                  demonstrate the necessity for directly dating hominid remains.”
                                  Could they have seen it?
                                  They measured the material themselves, with two methods (uranium-series
                                  and electron spin resonance) that can reach far beyond radiocarbon. But
                                  they also wrote that “some minor uranium mobilization may have occurred
                                  in the past”: uranium moving in or out of bone can change the answer.
                                  They did not find the remains; they worked in a laboratory, decades later.
                                  Why might they say it?
                                  To fix a date by testing the remains themselves rather than the sand around
                                  them. A very old date also supported their wider ideas about early human
                                  history. Students can ask: does dating the thing itself always beat dating
                                  what it was found in?
                                  Source. A. Thorne, R. Grün, G. Mortimer, N. A. Spooner, J. J. Simpson, M. McCulloch, L.
                                  Taylor and D. Curnoe, “Australia’s oldest human remains: age of the Lake Mungo 3
                                  skeleton,” Journal of Human Evolution 36, no. 6 (1999), pp. 591–612. Quoted from the
                                  published abstract. The image is a document silhouette, not a facsimile.

                                  What did they say they saw? · Could they really have seen it? · Why might they say it?

Jim Bowler and colleagues
                                 Geologist who found both sets of remains, with dating scientists · Nature, 20
                                 February 2003

                                 The geologist who knew the lunette best, returning with a large new set of
                                 sand dates.
                                 What they said
                                 “Here we report a new series of 25 optical ages showing that both burials
                                 occurred at 40 ± 2 kyr ago and that humans were present at Lake Mungo by
A document silhouette, not a
                                 50–46 kyr ago.” They wrote that “this new chronology corrects previous
  facsimile. Nature, 2003.       estimates for human burials at this important site.”
                                 Could they have seen it?
                                 Bowler found both sets of remains and had studied the lunette’s layers for
                                 decades. The team dated the sand in many places and checked that the ages
                                 ran in order, oldest at the bottom. But OSL dates the sand, not the people.
                                 A date for the remains depends on reading correctly which layer they were
                                 placed in.
                                 Why might they say it?
                                 To correct earlier dates, including the 62,000-year result, with many
                                 samples instead of a few. The paper also links people at the lake to a
                                 changing climate. Students can ask whether 25 dates from the sand
                                 outweigh direct dates from the remains, or whether they answer a different
                                 question.
                                 Source. J. M. Bowler, H. Johnston, J. M. Olley, J. R. Prescott, R. G. Roberts, W. Shawcross
                                 and N. A. Spooner, “New ages for human occupation and climatic change at Lake Mungo,
                                 Australia,” Nature 421 (2003), pp. 837–840. Quoted from the published abstract. The image
                                 is a document silhouette, not a facsimile.

A document silhouette, not a

facsimile. National Museum       archaeological dating techniques, scientists have dated the remains to

My finding
LAKE MUNGO · YEAR 7 · DECIDE

The three witness cards are the 1999 dating team, the 2003 dating team, and the National Museum of Australia.
Further questions — the four clocks, what is being dated, and who decides about ancestors — are in Super Sleuths.

You have a constructed notebook, a short agreed file, and three witnesses. The opening page is
not a historical document. Say how old you think the oldest evidence at Lake Mungo is, and
explain why the dates changed. “We can’t know” is an honest finding when methods disagree.
Do not invent a number the sources do not give.

How old is the oldest evidence at Lake Mungo, and why did the answer
keep changing?
Circle one: About 40,000 years: the 2003 dates are the best · About 62,000 years: the 1999 direct
dates are the best · People were at the lake earlier than the oldest remains · We can’t know an
exact age, but every method says tens of thousands of years · We can’t know, from this file ·
Another finding, written below


  MY FINDING
  My finding. ________________________________________________
  ______________________________________________________________
  The one piece of evidence that most changed my mind. ________
  ______________________________________________________________
  What I still can’t know. ___________________________________
  ______________________________________________________________




Why it still matters
Lake Mungo changed what Australians knew about the deep past, and it changed how scientists
date it. The file is open because each new method gave a new answer, and because a museum
label has to choose one. Who decides what happens to ancestors, and what science may still ask
of them, is a question about the present.

pages.text:
LAKE MUNGO · YEAR 7 · SUPER SLEUTHS
Super Sleuths
Go further only if you want to. Amber marks what is still disputed, or what later writers added. Lake
Mungo is on the Country of the Barkindji (Paakantji), Ngiyampaa and Mutthi Mutthi peoples. This file
shows no images of remains and does not describe burials.
Open these investigations in the app: robmac10.github.io/lake-mungo-case/#sleuth


 STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
 1. The notebook is written for this file
 The typed page is a constructed student voice in front of a whiteboard. The narrator and the teacher
 are not historical people. The three numbers (about 26,000, 62,000 and 40,000) are rounded from
 the agreed file.
 Question. Which of the three numbers in the notebook is rounded the most, and does the rounding
 change the story?




 2. Four clocks
 Radiocarbon counts carbon-14 in once-living material, and stops working much beyond about
 50,000 years. Uranium-series dating measures uranium and its decay products, which can soak into
 bone after burial. Electron spin resonance (ESR) measures radiation damage that builds up in tooth
 enamel. OSL measures energy stored in sand grains since they were last in sunlight.
 Question. For each clock, what exactly is being dated, and what could make it run fast or slow?




 STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
 3. Dating the remains, or the sand?
 The 1999 team argued for dating remains directly. The 2003 team dated the layers of the lunette in
 two lines, called transects, and checked that the ages were in order. Both methods need assumptions:
 about uranium moving, or about which layer the remains belong to.
 Question. Which assumption would you rather rely on, and why?




 STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER


                         Reopen the Record: Australian Histories · sample ·   247

pages.alt: Page 248. Lake Mungo. 4. A museum rounds the numbers The National Museum page says Mungo Lady is 40,000 to 42,000 years old, and that humans arrived at the lake about 40,000 years ago. The 2003 paper says people were
pages.text:
4. A museum rounds the numbers
The National Museum page says Mungo Lady is 40,000 to 42,000 years old, and that humans
arrived at the lake about 40,000 years ago. The 2003 paper says people were present by 50,000 to
46,000 years ago. The museum also reports about 460 human footprints found near the lake in
2003, dated to about 20,000 years ago.
Question. Is a museum wrong to round, or is it doing a different job from a scientific paper?




STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
5. Who decides about ancestors?
Mungo Lady was returned in 1992 and Mungo Man in 2017. The Australian National University
apologised to Elders for the hurt the removal caused. In 2022 the Australian Government approved a
reburial proposal supported by the Willandra Lakes Region Aboriginal Advisory Group. Some
Traditional Owners and some scientists wanted a keeping place instead. These are public facts; this
file does not take a side.
Question. Why might the people whose ancestors these are see the question “how old?” differently
from the scientists who asked it?




6. Sure, maybe, or a guess?
Sure: remains were found at Lake Mungo in 1968 and 1974; different methods have given ages from
about 20,000 to 62,000 years; the 2003 study gave about 40,000 years for both and placed people at
the lake by 50,000–46,000 years ago; both have been returned to Country. Maybe: which date is
closest to the truth. A guess: an exact year. The opener is not a source.
Question. Write a finding of no more than five sentences, and mark each sentence sure, maybe, or a
guess.




                        Reopen the Record: Australian Histories · sample ·   248

Teacher Note
LAKE MUNGO · YEAR 7 · TEACHER NOTE


This note is for the teacher. It is not a student page.


What’s true about the opener
The typographic page is a constructed student notebook, marked Imagined. It is not a historical
document and it quotes no one. Its three numbers are rounded from the published estimates in
the agreed file: radiocarbon estimates of about 20,000–26,000 years for Mungo Lady, the 1999
estimate of 62,000 ± 6,000 years for Mungo Man, and the 2003 estimate of 40,000 ± 2,000
years.


Curriculum
Year 7 History, Deep time history of Australia. Lead code AC9HH7K08 (methods and sources of
evidence used by historians and archaeologists, and the importance of conserving remains,
material culture and heritage). Also AC9HH7K07 (cultural obligations of First Nations
Australians about significant heritage sites, including ancestral remains, and the role of
collaboration) and AC9HH7K03. Codes checked against the v9 Year 7 History content
descriptions.


Country, ancestors, and care
This file names the ancestors only as public records do, with their public names. It uses no
images of remains, quotes no description of burial practices, and avoids the museum and
journal phrases that describe them. Repatriation and reburial are mentioned only as public fact.
Traditional Owners have held different views about reburial and about a keeping place; living
people on both sides have spoken publicly, and the file does not quote them or take a side.
Teachers should follow the protocols of the Barkindji (Paakantji), Ngiyampaa and Mutthi
Mutthi peoples, NSW National Parks guidance for Mungo National Park, and the AIATSIS Code
of Ethics.


Source conflicts, flagged
Ages for the same remains range from about 20,000 to 62,000 years across the published
record. The 2003 paper argues it corrects the earlier dates; the 1999 authors argued for direct
dating. The National Museum’s “about 40,000 years” for human arrival is younger than the
2003 paper’s “by 50–46 kyr ago.” Spellings vary across public sources (Paakantji or Barkindji;
Ngiyampaa or Ngyiampaa).

IMAGINED Written for this case, based on real events, not a real document.
                                                                            Library, back table
                      A constructed notebook · not a historical document
The ship’s own journal is lost. Nobody has it. Nobody has had it
for hundreds of years.
So what we know about the Duyfken comes from other people. An
English captain who heard a story from a ship’s master who had
heard it in Banda. A Dutch captain who sailed past the same
river seventeen years later. A council in Batavia writing a
summary for the next expedition.
And a map. A later copy, found in a library in Vienna.
Everyone agrees men died. Nobody in my pile of papers agrees on
why.

  The people who were standing on the beach have their
        own account. It isn’t mine to write down.

A NOTE BEFORE YOU READ
  The Duyfken reached the west coast of Cape York Peninsula, including Wik Country. This
  investigation acknowledges the Wik peoples and the other Traditional Owners of that coast, and uses
  only published, cited public records. Wik families hold their own account of 1606. It is not retold
  here; it belongs to them. Some Dutch and English records use words for First Peoples that are
  offensive today; they appear only where a source is quoted, and are cut where possible. If something
  here should be corrected, please tell the teacher who shared this investigation. A note for teachers is
  at the end of the case.




THE DUYFKEN, 1606 · YEAR 8 · READ
The Duyfken on Cape York, 1606
What happened when the Duyfken’s men went ashore in 1606?


What is agreed
Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber, used in Super Sleuths, marks what is still disputed or was
added later.


  In November 1605 the small Dutch East India Company (VOC) ship Duyfken (‘little dove’), with
  Willem Janszoon as skipper, left Bantam in Java to explore ‘Nova Guinea’ and look for trade and
  gold.




  In late February and early March 1606 the Duyfken sailed down the west coast of Cape York
  Peninsula, in what is now Queensland, charting about 197 nautical miles (about 365 kilometres)
  of coast. This is the first recorded European contact with the Australian continent. The crew
  seem to have thought it was part of New Guinea.




  The crew went ashore more than once. Some of them were killed. The ship turned back at a
  point named Cape Keerweer (‘turn back’), on Wik Country, and returned to Banda.




  The Duyfken’s own journal does not survive. A later copy of its chart was found in a library in
  Vienna in 1933. It is the oldest known map of any part of Australia.




  What happened ashore is known from later reports: an English captain’s diary of 1606, a Dutch

Three witnesses
THE DUYFKEN, 1606 · YEAR 8 · ASK


Each witness is a real person, or a real set of words from the record. A period portrait is used
where one exists and is free to reuse. Otherwise you will see a plain silhouette, not a likeness.
Ask the same three questions of each.

                                    John Saris, reporting Nakhoda Tingall
                                    English East India Company merchant at Bantam, 1605–1609 · Diary printed in
                                    Purchas his Pilgrimes, 1625 · Died 1643

                                    An English merchant who wrote down news brought by a ship’s master
                                    from Banda, about three months after the voyage.
                                    What they said
                                    On 18 November 1605: “heere departed a small Pinnasse of the Flemmings,
                                    for the discovery of the Land called Nova Guinea which, as it is said,
  A silhouette, not a likeness.
                                    affordeth great store of Gold.” On 15 June 1606, of the news from Banda:
  No portrait of John Saris is      “He told me that the Flemmings Pinasse which went upon discovery for
        used in this file.          Nova Ginny, was returned to Banda, having found the Iland: but in sending
                                    their men on shoare to intreate of Trade, there were nine of them killed by
                                    the Heathens … So they were constrained to returne, finding no good to be
                                    done there.”
                                    Could they have seen it?
                                    Saris was at Bantam, not on the ship or on the beach. He heard the news
                                    from a ship’s master, who had heard it at Banda. It is the earliest surviving
                                    report, written within months, but it is at least third-hand. It does not say
                                    where the men were killed; “nine” could cover more than one landing, or
                                    more than one place.
                                    Why might they say it?
                                    To keep his own company informed about its Dutch rivals. “To intreate of
                                    Trade” is how the news described the landings; it is not proof of what the
                                    crew did. The cut words are an insult Saris’s source used about the people
                                    on the shore. Students can ask what a report like this is likely to leave out.
                                    Source. John Saris, “Observations … at Bantam,” in Samuel Purchas, Hakluytus Posthumus,
                                    or Purchas his Pilgrimes (London, 1625), entries for 18 November 1605 and 15 June 1606
                                    (Old Style; 28 November 1605 and 25 June 1606 by the modern calendar). Quoted from J. E.
                                    Heeres, The Part Borne by the Dutch in the Discovery of Australia 1606–1765 (London,
                                    1899). The image is a silhouette, not a likeness.

pages.alt: Page 257. The Duyfken. Jan Carstenszoon Commander of the VOC ships Pera and Arnhem · Sailed the same coast in 1623 · Journal, translated by J. E. Heeres, 1899 A Dutch captain who passed the same river seventeen years
pages.text:
Jan Carstenszoon
                                  Commander of the VOC ships Pera and Arnhem · Sailed the same coast in 1623 ·
                                  Journal, translated by J. E. Heeres, 1899

                                  A Dutch captain who passed the same river seventeen years later, and wrote
                                  down what he had been told and what he guessed.
                                  What they said
                                  On 11 May 1623: “in the afternoon we sailed past a large river (which the
                                  men of the Duifken went up with a boat in 1606, and where one of them
A silhouette, not a likeness.
                                  was killed by the arrows of the …).” In a note, of the people they met
     No portrait of Jan           between 13° and 11° south: “they are also acquainted with muskets, of
    Carstenszoon exists.          which they would seem to have experienced the fatal effect when in 1606
                                  the men of the Duyffken made a landing here.”
                                  Could they have seen it?
                                  Carstenszoon was on this coast and in some of the same places, but
                                  seventeen years later. He did not see 1606. He probably knew of the river
                                  from the Duyfken’s chart or reports. His note about muskets is his own
                                  guess from how people met his crew. His own journal shows his men seized
                                  people and fired on them, so he had reasons to explain hostility as
                                  something others started.
                                  Why might they say it?
                                  To report his voyage to the Company. His journal shows that in 1606 there
                                  was killing on both sides: one Dutchman by arrows, and, he believed, local
                                  people by musket fire. Students can ask why the same record names the
                                  dead Dutchman’s weapon but not the number of local people killed.
                                  Source. Journal of Jan Carstenszoon, voyage of the Pera and Arnhem, 1623, entries for 11
                                  May and the note after 15 May 1623, in J. E. Heeres, The Part Borne by the Dutch in the
                                  Discovery of Australia 1606–1765 (London, 1899). The image is a silhouette, not a likeness.

                                 The Company’s own summary of the Duyfken voyage, written thirty-eight

                                 “the first was undertaken in the year 1606 with the Yacht ’t Duyffken … it
A document silhouette, not a     being only ascertained that vast regions were for the greater part
facsimile. VOC instructions,     uncultivated, and certain parts inhabited by … [people] who slew some of

                                 our sailors, so that no information was obtained touching the exact
                                 situation of the country and regarding the commodities obtainable and in
                                 demand there; our men having by want of provisions and other necessaries,
                                 been compelled to return and give up the discovery they had begun, only
                                 registering in their chart with the name of Cape Keer-weer the extreme

                                 Could they have seen it?
                                 The Council had the Company’s papers, possibly including the Duyfken’s

                                 voyage. It gives two reasons for turning back: the killing, and running out of
                                 supplies.

                                 To brief Tasman, and to explain why earlier voyages had found “no

                                 company looking for places to profit from. The cut words are insults the
                                 Council used. Students can ask what this summary chooses to blame, and

THE DUYFKEN, 1606 · YEAR 8 · DECIDE

The three witness cards are John Saris (reporting Nakhoda Tingall), Jan Carstenszoon, and the Council at
Batavia. Further questions — the lost journal, “first”, and what the museum says — are in Super Sleuths.

You have a constructed notebook, a short agreed file, and three witnesses. The opening page is
not a historical document. Say what you think happened when the Duyfken’s men went ashore,
and how sure you can be. “We can’t know” is an honest finding when the main record is lost. Do
not invent events, numbers or words that the sources do not give.

What happened when the Duyfken’s men went ashore in 1606?
Circle one: Men landed to trade, and were attacked · The crew did something that caused the
fighting · There was killing on both sides, and the records tell only the Dutch side · They turned
back because of the deaths and low supplies · We can’t know, from these records, what started it ·

Why it still matters
The Duyfken’s visit is the first recorded meeting between Europeans and people on the
Australian continent, and it was violent. The file is open because the ship’s own journal is lost,
the surviving reports are second-hand or later, and they were written by people who had
reasons to tell it their way. The people who were on the beach have their own account, and it is
theirs to share.

  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  1. The notebook is written for this file
  The typed page is a constructed student voice. The narrator is not a historical person. The facts in it
  (the lost journal, Saris, Carstenszoon, the Batavia council, the chart copy found in Vienna) come from
  the agreed file and the witness cards.
  Question. The narrator says the beach people’s account “isn’t mine to write down.” Why might a
  historian make that choice?




  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  2. The lost journal
  In 1618 the VOC wrote that the voyage was “amply set forth in their journals.” Those journals have
  not been found. The copy of the Duyfken’s chart, made about 1670, is the closest thing to the ship’s
  own record.
  Question. If one day the journal turned up, which of your answers would you expect to change, and
  which would stay?




  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  3. What the museum says
  The National Museum of Australia says the crew turned back “after some of them were killed in a
  skirmish with the Wik people. The conflict arose because the Duyfken’s crew were trying to abduct
  members of the tribe.” Its page does not say which source this comes from.
  Question. None of the three witnesses in this file says the crew tried to abduct anyone. What kind of
  source could?




                          Reopen the Record: Australian Histories · sample ·   260

pages.alt: Page 261. The Duyfken. STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER 4. Nine, or one? Saris’s report says nine men were killed. Carstenszoon mentions one man killed by arrows at a river. The Batavia council says “some of our sailors.”
pages.text:
STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
4. Nine, or one?
Saris’s report says nine men were killed. Carstenszoon mentions one man killed by arrows at a river.
The Batavia council says “some of our sailors.” The three numbers may describe different landings, or
a total and a single event.
Question. Can all three numbers be true at once? What would have to be true for that?




STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
5. First?
The Duyfken’s visit is the first recorded European contact with the Australian continent. People from
Makassar, New Guinea and the Torres Strait islands had contact with the continent too, and First
Peoples had lived there for tens of thousands of years. “First” in these sources means first written
down by Europeans.
Question. Rewrite the sentence “Janszoon discovered Australia in 1606” so that it is accurate.




6. Sure, maybe, or a guess?
Sure: the Duyfken charted part of the west coast of Cape York in 1606; some of the crew were killed;
the ship turned back at Cape Keerweer; the journal is lost. Maybe: how many died, where, and that
local people were shot. A guess: what the crew intended when they landed, unless a source says. The
opener is not a source.
Question. Write a finding of no more than five sentences, and mark each sentence sure, maybe, or a
guess.

Teacher Note
THE DUYFKEN, 1606 · YEAR 8 · TEACHER NOTE


This note is for the teacher. It is not a student page.


What’s true about the opener
The typographic page is a constructed student notebook, marked Imagined. It is not a historical
document. Its facts come from the agreed file and witness cards.


Curriculum
Year 8 History, Empires and expansions, with the Dutch East India Company as the expanding
power. Lead code AC9HH8K08 (a significant event, development, turning point or challenge
that contributed to continuity and change related to the empire and/or expansion). Also
AC9HH8K09 (the experiences and perspectives of rulers and of subject peoples, and how the
interaction between power and/or authority relates to the empire and/or expansion) and
AC9HH8K11 (interpretations about the society and events, and/or individuals and/or groups
connected to the empire and/or expansion). Honest note: the encounter also fits the Year 9
study of contact between First Nations Peoples and Europeans (AC9HH9K03: the causes and
effects of European contact and extension of settlement, including their impact on the First
Nations Peoples of Australia). It is listed under Year 8 at the author’s request.


Country, and care
The landings were on the west coast of Cape York Peninsula; Cape Keerweer is on Wik Country.
Wik people hold an oral account of the Duyfken’s visit, recorded and published in the 1970s and
discussed in later public writing, including Monash University’s “1623 Project.” It is deliberately
not retold or summarised in this file, because it belongs to Wik families. Teachers who wish to
include it should use a published, community-endorsed version and follow the AIATSIS Code of
Ethics. The VOC and English records use slurs for First Peoples; these are cut with an ellipsis
(…), as the National Museum of Australia also does, and one cut is replaced with [people]. The
1623 journal records Carstenszoon’s men seizing and shooting local people; this is stated, not
described.


Source conflicts, flagged
Number killed: nine (Saris), one at a river (Carstenszoon), “some” (Batavia, 1644). Cause: “to
intreate of Trade” (Saris) against “trying to abduct” (National Museum of Australia, no source
given on its page). Reasons for turning back: deaths alone (Saris) against deaths and lack of
supplies (Batavia, 1644). Dates: Saris used the Old Style calendar, ten days behind the modern
one. The river Carstenszoon mentions is usually identified with the Wenlock River.

IMAGINED Written for this case, based on real events, not a real document.
                                                                    Homework, kitchen table
                       A constructed notebook · not a historical document
Somebody hammered a dinner plate flat and scratched words into
it.
That is the whole message. A date, a ship, five men’s names, and
where they were going next. Then they nailed it to a post and
sailed away.
Eighty-one years later another captain found it, took it, and
left a copy with his own names added. The first plate is in
Amsterdam now. The copy is in Fremantle. It went to France first.
Our textbook says first. A museum website says second. The plate
itself doesn’t say either.

    I read the names again. None of them is the name of
                 anyone who lived there.

A NOTE BEFORE YOU READ
  Dirk Hartog Island is in Shark Bay, on Malgana Country. This investigation acknowledges the
  Malgana people as Traditional Owners, and uses only published, cited public records. The 1616 plate
  records a ship’s visit. It says nothing about the people whose Country it was. If something here
  should be corrected, please tell the teacher who shared this investigation. A note for teachers is at the
  end of the case.




DIRK HARTOG’S PLATE, 1616 · YEAR 8 · READ
Dirk Hartog’s plate, 1616
What does a flattened pewter plate prove?


What is agreed
Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber, used in Super Sleuths, marks what is still disputed or was
added later.


  On 25 October 1616 the Dutch East India Company (VOC) ship Eendracht, with Dirk Hartog as
  skipper, reached the island now called Dirk Hartog Island, in Shark Bay, Western Australia. The
  crew stayed about three days and sailed on 27 October towards Bantam, in Java.




  The crew flattened a pewter plate, scratched an inscription into it, and nailed it to a post on high
  ground at the north end of the island, a place now called Cape Inscription.




  The inscription, in translation, reads: “1616 the 25 October is here arrived the ship Eendraght of
  Amsterdam the uppermerchant Gillis Miebais of Liege skipper Dirck Hatichs of Amsterdam. The
  27 ditto [we] set sail for Bantum the undermerchant Jan Stins, the first mate Pieter Dookes van
  Bil. Anno 1616.” (Western Australian Museum translation.)




  In February 1697 another VOC expedition, under Willem de Vlamingh in the Geelvinck, found
  Hartog’s plate. De Vlamingh took it to Batavia (now Jakarta), and it was sent on to the
  Netherlands. It is now in the Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam. He left a new pewter plate in its place,
  copying Hartog’s words and adding his own.




  In 1801 a French expedition found de Vlamingh’s plate; Captain Jacques Hamelin had it put

Why it still matters
Two pieces of flattened pewter are among the most famous objects in Australian history. The
file is open because the words on them are short, because later people added meanings such as
“first” and “discovery,” and because the plates are silent about the Malgana. What an object is

Hartog Island is on Malgana Country. This file uses published public records only.
Open these investigations in the app: robmac10.github.io/hartog-plate-case/#sleuth


  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  1. The notebook is written for this file
  The typed page is a constructed student voice. The narrator is not a historical person. The facts in it
  (the hammered plate, five names, eighty-one years, Amsterdam, Fremantle, France) come from the
  agreed file.
  Question. The narrator notices whose names are missing. Is that a historical observation, a feeling, or
  both?




  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  2. First, or second?
  The Western Australian Museum calls Hartog’s landing “the first recorded landfall of a European on
  the coast of Australia.” The National Museum of Australia says he was “the first European to set foot
  on the shores of Western Australia, and only the second to record encountering the Australian
  continent,” after Willem Janszoon in the Duyfken in 1606. The same Western Australian Museum
  page also says Hartog made “one of the first recorded landfalls by a European on the West Australian
  coastline.”
  Question. Can both statements be true? What exactly would “first” have to mean for each one to be
  right?




  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  3. 2 February or 4 February?
  The Western Australian Museum says de Vlamingh’s first mate found Hartog’s plate on 2 February
  1697. De Vlamingh’s own plate says the Geelvinck “arrived” on 4 February. Ships often lay off a coast
  before the official arrival was recorded.
  Question. Does a two-day difference matter to the question this case asks? When would it matter?

pages.alt: Page 274. Dirk Hartog’s plate. STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER 4. Who found it in 1801? The French expedition’s accounts differ. The Western Australian Museum says several crew, including Louis de Freycinet, found de Vlamingh’s
pages.text:
STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
4. Who found it in 1801?
The French expedition’s accounts differ. The Western Australian Museum says several crew,
including Louis de Freycinet, found de Vlamingh’s plate and gave it to Captain Hamelin, who had it
put back. The National Museum says de Freycinet found it. The Western Australian Museum also
notes that the French accounts disagree about whether the plate went back on its old post or a new
one.
Question. Why do small details, such as who picked something up, drift between retellings?




STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
5. An island described as uninhabited
The National Museum describes the island in 1616 as “rugged and uninhabited.” The plate says
nothing about people. Shark Bay is Malgana Country, and the Malgana are recognised today as
Traditional Owners of the Shark Bay World Heritage Area with the Nanda and Yinggarda peoples.
Question. What is the difference between “no one was seen” and “no one belonged there”? Which one
can a plate prove?




6. Sure, maybe, or a guess?
Sure: the Eendracht reached the island on 25 October 1616 and left on 27 October; the crew left an
inscribed pewter plate; de Vlamingh removed it in 1697 and left a copy; the original is in the
Rijksmuseum and the copy in Fremantle. Maybe: whether the landing was the first or second
recorded European landing in Australia. A guess: what the crew saw, felt or met. The opener is not a
source.
Question. Write a finding of no more than five sentences, and mark each sentence sure, maybe, or a
guess.

Teacher Note
DIRK HARTOG’S PLATE, 1616 · YEAR 8 · TEACHER NOTE


This note is for the teacher. It is not a student page.


What’s true about the opener
The typographic page is a constructed student notebook, marked Imagined. It is not a historical
document. Its facts come from the agreed file. “Our textbook says first” is a constructed line
about a common claim, not a quotation from any named textbook.


Curriculum
Year 8 History, Empires and expansions, with the Dutch East India Company as the expanding
power. Lead code AC9HH8K08 (a significant event, development, turning point or challenge
that contributed to continuity and change related to the empire and/or expansion). Also
AC9HH8K10 (the role and achievements of a significant individual and/or group connected to
the empire and/or expansion) and AC9HH8K11 (interpretations about the society and events,
and/or individuals and/or groups connected to the empire and/or expansion). Codes checked
against the v9 Year 8 History content descriptions.


Country, and care
Dirk Hartog Island is on Malgana Country; the Malgana name for the island is given in some
public sources, but it is not used here without a Malgana source. No Malgana stories are retold.
The file’s point about silence is about the record, not a claim about what happened on the island
in 1616. Teachers wishing to add Malgana perspectives should seek resources approved by the
Malgana Aboriginal Corporation and follow the AIATSIS Code of Ethics.


Source conflicts, flagged
First or second recorded European landing (WA Museum against National Museum). 2 or 4
February 1697 (WA Museum narrative against the 1697 plate). Who found the plate in 1801
(WA Museum against National Museum). The inscription’s spellings differ between
transcriptions (Gillis or Gilles; Mibais or Miebais; Dookes or Doores; Lvik, Lvck or Luick, for
Liège). The plate inscription spells the skipper “Dirck Hatichs.”


Pictures
The two plate images are from J. S. Battye (ed.), The Cyclopedia of Western Australia (1912): a
photograph of Hartog’s plate and a drawing of de Vlamingh’s inscription, public domain
(Wikimedia Commons, from the National Library of Australia). The WA Museum card uses a
document silhouette. No portrait of Hartog or de Vlamingh is used. The QR emblem is a drawn
plate, not a photograph.

IMAGINED Written for this case, based on real events, not a real document.
                                                                   In front of a museum case
                      A constructed notebook · not a historical document
The label says dried trepang. It looks like a burnt stick. People
sailed for weeks to collect these.
Every December, the label says, boats came from Makassar with
the monsoon wind, and every April they went home. For maybe a
hundred and fifty years. The fishermen camped on the beaches,
boiled and dried the trepang, and worked with the people whose
Country it was.
Then it stopped. One page I read says the new Australian
Government banned it. Another says it was a government in
Adelaide. Somebody had to sign something.

  I keep looking for the name on the paper. The case is
                       still open.

pages.text:
A NOTE BEFORE YOU READ
  The Makassan voyages reached the coast of Arnhem Land, Yolŋu Country. This investigation
  acknowledges the Yolŋu people and uses only published, cited public records. It does not retell Yolŋu
  stories, songs or ceremonies about the Makassans; those belong to Yolŋu communities. If something
  here should be corrected, please tell the teacher who shared this investigation. A note for teachers is
  at the end of the case.




MAKASSAN TREPANGERS, 1803–1907 · YEAR 8 · READ
Makassan trepangers in Arnhem Land, 1700s–
1907
Why did the Makassan voyages to Arnhem Land end, and who decided?


What is agreed
Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber, used in Super Sleuths, marks what is still disputed or was
added later.


  From at least the 1700s until 1907, fleets of boats called praus sailed from Makassar, on the
  island of Sulawesi (now in Indonesia), to the coast of Arnhem Land, which the visitors called
  Marege’. They came with the north-west monsoon about December and left about April.




  They came for trepang, also called sea cucumber or bêche-de-mer, which they gathered, boiled
  and dried, and which was sold on to buyers in China.




  On 17 February 1803 Matthew Flinders, commanding HMS Investigator, met six praus at the
  islands he named the English Company’s Islands. Their leader was named Pobassoo. Flinders’
  Malay cook interpreted.




  The visitors met, traded and worked with Yolŋu people. They brought metal tools, cloth, tobacco
  and words still used today. They did not settle in Arnhem Land.




  From 1863 the Northern Territory was governed by South Australia. In the 1880s the South
  Australian government began to charge the Makassan fleets customs duties and a licence fee.

pages.alt: Page 281. The Makassan trepangers. The Commonwealth took over the Northern Territory on 1 January 1911. In 1906 the government decided to stop issuing licences to the Makassan trepangers. The last prau from Makassar came to Arnhem
pages.text:
The Commonwealth took over the Northern Territory on 1 January 1911.




In 1906 the government decided to stop issuing licences to the Makassan trepangers. The last
prau from Makassar came to Arnhem Land in 1907. Public sources disagree about which
government made the decision, and why.

Three witnesses
MAKASSAN TREPANGERS, 1803–1907 · YEAR 8 · ASK


Each witness is a real person, or a real set of words from the record. A period portrait is used
where one exists and is free to reuse. Otherwise you will see a plain silhouette, not a likeness.
Ask the same three questions of each.

                                   Matthew Flinders, reporting Pobassoo
                                   Commander of HMS Investigator · Met the praus at the English Company’s
                                   Islands, 17–19 February 1803 · A Voyage to Terra Australis, 1814 · Died 1814

                                   An English navigator who wrote down what a Makassan captain told him,
                                   through an interpreter.
                                   What they said
                                   “The chief of the six prows was a short, elderly man, named Pobassoo.”
                                   “Pobassoo had made six or seven voyages from Macassar to this coast,
  Matthew Flinders, portrait
                                   within the preceding twenty years, and he was one of the first who came.”
    by Toussaint Antoine de        The trepang “is carried to Timor, and sold to the Chinese, who meet them
  Chazal. Public domain. No        there.” “They sometimes had skirmishes with the native inhabitants of the
  likeness of Pobassoo exists.
                                   coast.”
                                   Could they have seen it?
                                   Flinders was there, and he questioned the captains for two days. But almost
                                   everything he wrote about the fleet came from Pobassoo, through Flinders’
                                   cook. He saw one small part of the coast in one season. He could not see the
                                   earlier voyages, or the end of the trade a century later.
                                   Why might they say it?
                                   To report a trade that a British colony might one day want for itself. He
                                   wrote that a colony on the east coast “might perhaps derive considerable
                                   advantage from the trepang.” Students can ask what Pobassoo wanted
                                   Flinders to know, and what Flinders wanted his readers in London to think.
                                   Source. Matthew Flinders, A Voyage to Terra Australis (London, 1814), vol. 2, book 2,
                                   chapter 9 (text on Wikisource). Portrait by Toussaint Antoine de Chazal, about 1806–07,
                                   Wikimedia Commons (Google Art Project), public domain.

pages.text:
Alfred Searcy
                                  Sub-Collector of Customs at Port Darwin for fourteen years, from the 1880s · In
                                  Australian Tropics, first published 1907

                                  The South Australian customs officer who sailed along the coast to tell the
                                  Makassan captains they must now pay.
                                  What they said
                                  “Now that there was some chance of Europeans following suit, and with the
                                  idea of encouraging local trading on the coast, it was decided that the time
A silhouette, not a likeness.
                                  had come for the Malays to be placed on an equal footing with the local
No period portrait of Alfred      people, and to pay something towards the revenue of the country, to which
 Searcy is used in this file.     hitherto they had not contributed a penny.” “I made preparations for my
                                  first voyage down the coast to warn the masters of the proas that in future a
                                  licence would have to be paid, and also duty on the stores used on the
                                  coast.”
                                  Could they have seen it?
                                  He was the official who collected the money, and he sailed the coast himself
                                  from 1884. He could see the licences and the fleets. He was writing a lively
                                  memoir years later, and he does not say who in Adelaide made the decision.
                                  He left the Territory before the trade ended in 1906–07.
                                  Why might they say it?
                                  To explain and defend his own work, and to entertain readers at home. His
                                  claim that the visitors had taken “millions of pounds’ worth” from the coast
                                  is his own estimate, not a figure from the customs books. Students can ask
                                  how a tax collector’s view of the trade might differ from a Makassan
                                  captain’s, or a Yolŋu family’s.
                                  Source. Alfred Searcy, In Australian Tropics (London: George Robertson, first published
                                  1907; quoted from the third edition, 1909), pp. 12–13, text on the Internet Archive. No period
                                  portrait of Searcy is used here. The image is a silhouette, not a likeness.

                                 The Defining Moments page: “After 1901 the newly formed Australian

pages.text:
My finding
MAKASSAN TREPANGERS, 1803–1907 · YEAR 8 · DECIDE

The three witness cards are Matthew Flinders (reporting Pobassoo), Alfred Searcy, and the National Museum of
Australia. Further questions — when it began, who signed, and the last voyage — are in Super Sleuths.

You have a constructed notebook, a short agreed file, and three witnesses. The opening page is
not a historical document. Say why you think the voyages ended, and which government
decided. “We can’t know” is an honest finding when public sources disagree. Do not invent a
name or a document the sources do not give.

Why did the Makassan voyages to Arnhem Land end, and who decided?
Circle one: Licences and duties from the 1880s slowly ended it · The South Australian government
ended it in 1906, to favour local trepangers · The new Commonwealth ended it, to guard the border
· All of these played a part · We can’t know, from this file, who made the final decision ·
Another finding, written below


  MY FINDING
  My finding. ________________________________________________
  ______________________________________________________________
  The one piece of evidence that most changed my mind. ________
  ______________________________________________________________
  What I still can’t know. ___________________________________
  ______________________________________________________________




Why it still matters
Long before 1788, the north coast was part of a trading world that reached Makassar and China.
The file is open because the end of that world was decided on paper, far from the beaches, and
public accounts still disagree about whose paper it was. Who gets to decide who may come to a
coast, and for whose benefit, is not only a question about 1906.

MAKASSAN TREPANGERS, 1803–1907 · YEAR 8 · SUPER SLEUTHS
Super Sleuths
Go further only if you want to. Amber marks what is still disputed, or what later writers added. The
Makassan voyages reached Yolŋu Country. This file uses published public records only, and does not
retell Yolŋu stories or songs.
Open these investigations in the app: robmac10.github.io/makassan-case/#sleuth


  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  1. The notebook is written for this file
  The typed page is a constructed student voice in front of a museum case. The narrator is not a
  historical person. The facts in it (December and April, the camps, the 1906 disagreement) come from
  the agreed file. “Maybe a hundred and fifty years” is the narrator’s rough sum, not a source.
  Question. Which words in the notebook show the narrator is unsure, and is that a weakness or a
  strength?




  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  2. When did it begin?
  The National Museum says “from at least 1700.” Historians have long placed the first voyages in the
  first half of the 1700s. Pobassoo told Flinders in 1803 that he was “one of the first who came,” within
  the past twenty years, and one historian has reconsidered a start date of about 1780 on that basis.
  Question. How much weight can one captain’s memory, written down by someone else through an
  interpreter, carry?




  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  3. Who signed?
  South Australia governed the Northern Territory until 1 January 1911. The 2008 museum talk says
  “the government” decided in 1906. The museum’s later page says “the newly formed Australian
  Government.” A 2024 article in Australian Historical Studies, “The Macassan–Aboriginal
  relationship and the Commonwealth of Australia 1901–1906,” studies how the two governments
  dealt with the question.
  Question. What document would you need to see to settle who made the 1906 decision?




                          Reopen the Record: Australian Histories · sample ·   286

pages.alt: Page 287. The Makassan trepangers. STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER 4. Revenue, protection, or the border? Searcy gives revenue and “encouraging local trading.” The 2008 talk gives protecting “the local industry.” The Defining Moments
pages.text:
STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
4. Revenue, protection, or the border?
Searcy gives revenue and “encouraging local trading.” The 2008 talk gives protecting “the local
industry.” The Defining Moments page adds “territorial integrity.” These are three different reasons,
and they can all be true at once.
Question. Rank the three reasons from best supported to least supported by the witnesses in this file.




STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
5. The last voyage
The 2008 talk says only four praus came in the 1905–06 season, one captained by Using Daeng
Rangka, and that in 1907 he sailed again to check whether the ban was true. It was. He has an entry
in the Australian Dictionary of Biography.
Question. Why might a captain sail all that way to check a rule, instead of believing it?




6. Sure, maybe, or a guess?
Sure: praus sailed from Makassar to Arnhem Land for trepang for well over a century; Flinders met
Pobassoo in 1803; South Australia charged duties and licences from the 1880s; licences stopped in
1906 and the last prau came in 1907. Maybe: which government made the final decision, and its main
reason. A guess: what Yolŋu families thought of the ban. The opener is not a source.
Question. Write a finding of no more than five sentences, and mark each sentence sure, maybe, or a
guess.

Teacher Note
MAKASSAN TREPANGERS, 1803–1907 · YEAR 8 · TEACHER NOTE


This note is for the teacher. It is not a student page.


What’s true about the opener
The typographic page is a constructed student notebook, marked Imagined. It is not a historical
document. The museum label it describes is not quoted; the facts it gives come from the agreed
file. The National Museum of Australia does hold and display a dried trepang specimen, but the
opener does not claim to describe a particular case.


Curriculum
Listed as Year 8, Empires and expansions: AC9HH8K08 (a significant event, development,
turning point or challenge that contributed to continuity and change related to the empire
and/or expansion) and AC9HH8K07 (the significant social, religious, cultural, economic,
environmental and/or political features of different groups related to the empire and/or
expansion). The trade sat inside the wider Indonesian archipelago–China trading world of the
Dutch East India Company era. Honest note: by its dates (1803–1907) this case fits Year 9
better, in the Making and transforming the Australian nation depth study, especially
AC9HH9K06 and AC9HH9K07. It is listed under Year 8 at the author’s request.


Country, and care
The Makassan voyages are part of Yolŋu history, and Yolŋu communities hold songs,
ceremonies and stories about them. None of these are retold here, and no Yolŋu art is
reproduced. Flinders records “skirmishes” and that Pobassoo had been speared; violence on
both sides is part of the record and is not described further. Period words such as “Malays” and
“natives” appear only inside short quotations. Teachers wishing to add Yolŋu perspectives
should seek community-approved resources and follow the AIATSIS Code of Ethics.


Source conflicts, flagged
Start date: “from at least 1700” (NMA) against Pobassoo’s twenty years (Flinders). Decision-
maker in 1906: the Australian Government (NMA Defining Moments) against “the government”
in a talk that names South Australia as the Territory’s administrator (NMA, 2008). The 2024
Australian Historical Studies article should be read by teachers before choosing a side.
Spellings: Makassar for the place and Makasar for the people (NMA usage); Macassan in older
writing.
